text:
The official verdict is absolute Crap!

I'm a Commercial pilot (Complex piston singles) and I have followed this story from the beginning.  The official story is pathetic.  This will go down in history as one best examples of aviation bravery.

For this story to have the happy ending that it did, 3 things had to happen perfectly:

First, Cpt. Smit who while on the floor (being attacked with an axe!!!) thought "these are my last moments, but I cant let these people die" and somehow opened the cockpit door.  Without his bravery and determination, Everybody dies no question.

Second the passengers Yaniv and Yitzhack rushed the cockpit the minute they heard screams.  Dont minimize this.  Most people in a situation like this would freeze in their seats.  Not to mention getting the the front of the plane in a zero G nose over.  I'm assuming IDF training (mandatory for all Israelis) but even then excellent reactions under pressure.  By rushing to the front immediately, they were on the other side of the door the second that Cpt Smit opened it.  The IDF training also probably had a hand in their ability to rapidly neutralize the co-pilot.

Yaniv taking the stick and pulling out of the dive is critical simply because there was no time otherwise.  At the rate of decent by that point there is maybe 30s to impact if they keep diving (and they were already past Vne)  

However, contrary to popular male ego, a non pilot successfully recovering the plane has odds near zero.  Commercial aircraft are huge and have massive momentum.  Even in a small plane, if you are too heavy on the controls nothing happens for ten seconds, then next thing you know you are upside down.  The most likely outcome after a non-pilot pulling out of a dive would be overcontrolling and triggering a stall.  Fortunately (according to Yaniv's interview) the relief pilot took over just as he leveled the plane.  

The relief pilots being on board was fortunate, the relief pilot managing to take over the controls before Yaniv could trigger a stall was perfect timing.  The pilots were not just random pilots or random airline pilots, they were the relief crew which meant they had hundreds if not thousands of hours in that exact model.  Why is this important?  Because the co-pilot had smashed the instruments (once again from Yaniv's interview) and the rudder was damaged from exceeding Vne.  The relief pilots could handle this as a routine emergency, for a pilot unfamiliar with that airplane and instruments smashed it would be a insurmountable challenge.

Finally the Pilot who thought he was going to die was in luck because on board was a dentist.  A dental surgeon no less.  Not quite the same an ER doc, but enough to stop major arterial bleeding from multiple wounds.  

If somebody doesnt make a great movie out of this it would be a crime.  This is aviation history being made.

text: There is nothing more "it's all an illusion/ all life is a state of impermanence" than the Man City story. Crisis is when the truth overpowers the illusion. Go easy on the Man City fans. Their pain is unbearably real. It will feel like death. It is a collective ego death. It will illicit depression, grief and anger. It could have happened to any one of us at our clubs. It's too easy to say they are deluded. When your very sense of identity is under threat, when the past is revealed to have been a lie, your very sense of self is shattered and you will do anything to cling to it, fight for it. This happens to so many of us at some point in our life - the job, the relationship, the status, the external evidence that gives us a sense of value, will, at some point be challenged and bring upon us a crash in self worth and value. This is part of our journey here. It's why we age, why we lose, why we die. Everything is in a constant state of decay and loss - on the outside. The lesson is you are really here to focus on the inside - which never grows old, depreciates or dies. The Man City story is not new. It is very much part of the fabric of this world. When it happens collectively - to a fan base, a nation, a community, a culture, an ethnic group, a religion - it feels like the end of the world, because it really is the end of the world, the external world, the thing we have looked to for our sense of self and value. It is a death. A grief. A loss. But it is also the greatest tool for spiritual growth and expansion and I don't mean religion. True spiritual growth. The power that exists within you - not outside you. The delusion we accuse Man City fans of, is their ego death rattle. Give them space. They are, at some level, fighting tooth and nail to stay alive. We should not be cruel to them. We should be kind. Let them work through it. It is, after all, a catastrophe. They are football fans like us. We all love the game in the same way. Every one of us. It is such a beautiful game because of its simplicity and because of its wonder. Because of its universality. The stars in the game will come and go. Clubs will rise and fall. But the game will live on. Enjoyment in their demise is ghoulish. Be careful, it may not happen to your club but any one of us is one step away from it happening in our lives - the diagnosis, the job loss, the accident, the "out of the blue" circumstances that force us to look inwardly. The theft, the "bad luck", the changes outside our control. We are all on a journey of surrender and no life is free of it. I feel sorry for Man City fans. Truly sorry.

text:
Whether you are of any belief—Islam, Mormonism, Buddhism, Catholicism—or your religion is to “believe there is no God at all but me,” my desire is that we live in peace and dialogue as brothers and sisters in this fleshly existence, seeking to center our Faith on what is True.

I have friends of many different beliefs that do not square with my own, and they are kind and respectful and even endure my questioning of their beliefs. Sometimes iron must strike iron to make us sharper.

Having traveled the world and broken bread in so many beautiful cultures for more than two decades, and having discussed so many other beliefs and what they offer, one thing is clear: to have no faith in anything is a more hopeless existence.

And yet, while many religions do not agree, most share commonality on things that matter to us all—being true, being just, being kind, and loving one another with brotherly love.

If we cannot agree on some things, let us be satisfied with those precepts we can agree on, while extending patience to others who need more time to arrive at their own decision and place in eternity, however dire we feel that decision may be.

Love demands that we respect free choice, at least with respect to choosing what we believe.

Surely some cannot tolerate—and are even maddened by—any discussion of a possible spiritual state. Some blindly follow as if growing in their faith cannot tolerate being questioned.
You don’t have to be settled on any belief to offer some wisdom. Life experience alone has raised mankind up to believe in many things we call “the common good.”

I laughed when Elon Musk was asked what his philosophy for life was. He paused and said  “Strive to be less wrong. Whatever else, do that.”  He was quite right on that point.

My aim is simple—land on Faith so True it can endure any challenge, even though Faith does not require that every true thing can be fully known.

Even so, the residual risk of our eternal state does rest on some elements of “Faith” that we cannot see, test, or know—and not all “blind faith” is “untrue faith.”

Stay Faithful and True.

Superintelligence is starting to move from a distant thought experiment into a very public industry debate.

Palisade Research has published filmed interviews with current and former researchers from @OpenAI, @Google DeepMind and @Anthropic discussing their personal views on increasingly capable AI.

They do not all agree on the level or type of risk.
But that is exactly what makes the signal interesting.
Questions that used to sit mostly in research papers and closed safety discussions are now being discussed on camera by people who have worked inside frontier labs.

For teams building with frontier AI, the practical question is no longer only:
“How capable is the model?”
It is also:
→ What can it actually do?
→ Where does it fail?
→ How do we test those failure modes?
→ What controls are needed before deployment?
→ What evidence should exist before a capability claim becomes a production decision?

Capability without evaluation is still a claim.
Capability with evidence can be reviewed, compared and governed.

quoted_text:
.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

quoted_text:
@AllInBritney I’m a pretty stubborn person, so I drove to Vegas on Sep 30th and actually went to Venetian to collect evidence.

1. I went to the Venetian security department on Sep 30th around 3 ～4am and talked to three people there. I have all of their names. They helped me look up my name, Britney’s name, and Xuan’s name to see if there was any report connected to this. There was nothing.

2. In Britney’s Twitter, she said that at one point I secretly cashed out $106,250. I asked the Venetian poker room about my transactions. There are only two transactions under my name. (I’ll include evidence in the comment area).One was me coloring up $175k on June 7th, and the other was me cashing out $190,820 on June 9th. When I cashed out on June 9th, I was at the cage with five other players including Britney. 

3. I also have screenshots showing that on June 7th, right after the game, I was actually the first person who brought it up to Britney that the numbers felt off. Didn’t think much of it at the time just casually mentioned it. That’s why the next day she started asking everyone for their P/L. Again, some people didn’t even remember their exact P/L because they were too drunk. After adding up everyone’s already inaccurate P/L, the numbers were about $80k off.

At that point, I asked Britney TWICE to check the CCTV. I asked because I kinda knew she had this pattern of accusing people of stealing chips or misreporting numbers without enough evidence. Hank was not the only person she had been saying things about. So I was a bit worried and I didn’t want to leave anything unclear. She kept telling me, “There’s no need to,” and saying, “It’s definitely Big Mike or Rampage (because maybe they were too drunk to remember their exact P/L).” And then we just dropped it.

So if I had actually lied my numbers, why would I be the one to bring it up to Britney in the first place? Why would I ask her twice to go check the CCTV? That’s one of the biggest reasons I believe Britney knew from the very beginning that I never did anything shady. And that’s what makes this accusation so hard for me to get past. It’s also why I don’t feel like she deserves my money. Because at that point, it’s not just a misunderstanding. It felt malicious.

I put up with a lot from my friends. Usually I let a lot of things slide until it gets to a point where I no longer feel like I’m being treated like a friend. I didn’t just wake up one day and decide to blow this whole thing up for no reason. It took a lot for me to get to this point. You can call me petty or whatever for taking all of this public and turning it into some big cat fight if you want. But I’m not gonna let people walk all over me like that.

People keep saying, “All this over 18k?”Exactly. Maybe you should be asking Britney why she is trying so hard to accuse someone of stealing chips over “just 18k.”

It’s honestly ridiculous that I had to do all of this just to defend myself against something that basically came out of nowhere, based on a few words from different people. A lot of people talked about one part they personally saw, at one particular moment, from their own perspective. So sure, maybe you can go around and confidently say you didn’t lie and therefore you did nothing wrong. After all, you weren’t the one who actually drew the conclusion!

All of these separate pieces that were not enough to prove anything on their own got put together in a way that created a completely misleading picture like a montage. Every single clip can be real, but once you cut them together in a certain way, they can tell a story that isn’t true at all. And you all knew how much weight your words carried. You knew what could happen when people heard these things coming from you. So c’mon, stop pretending that you had nothing to do with this. You know damn well you played a part in it. You’re all some fucked-up adults. 

多行不义必自毙。夜路走多了总会遇到鬼的。

text:
The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine

author: madhavanmalolan

text:
Good thoughts but (so far) nothing has changed my $PRL thesis.

Let's put some of it in writing tho...

1/ Everyone seems to agree that matmuls can be proof of work. Great this isn't contentious. Usually big things like this are contentious.

2/ Useful work is not enforced by code but is a limit condition from the economics. One of my first metaphors for PRL was an "industrial byproduct". Coins CAN be mined intentionally but once the industrial engines are running at scale it won't be economic. 

There are many products today that are byproducts of other industrial processes (asphalt, whey protein, fly ash, bunker). PRL is roughly one of those that also happens to be supply constrained, energy secure, and transferable over a wire (e.g. suitable as a money).

Now you COULD make whey protein or asphalt solo without the other processes, but it doesn't make economic sense. Same as solo mining PRL in the future.

3/ I have lots of models on https://t.co/JtCNxCUWsb, but none of it is really worth arguing about until fp8 is out. 

Ilans keynote talk on Pearl Research YouTube channel explains the core limit today (pre-fp8) and why there is so much confusion.

https://t.co/doflyaD3Hw

PRL today works on integer math which requires models quantized to 7 bit integers. That's a weird custom quantization. Quantizing lowers model intelligence and duplex efficiency.

FP8 kernel, once released, will let PRL drop into existing AI stacks. No quantization and far less overhead means PRL mining is very close to free when doing inference. That means some inference providers likely to join, test mining profitability, and harden the network.

4/ A useful way to think of overhead, not sure if it's right, is that 1/8 bits is 0.125 which is the 12.5% efficiency loss we see from PRL mining today during inference.

Once the PRL noise is mixed INTO floats, that can go way lower because floats don't need to express noise in 1/8th of the whole information package.

5/ At that point when fp8 is out, Rafael Pass economic game theory begins to play out. Difficulty will go up as new miners join, cost to solo mine will increase faster (I think) than cost to duplex mine. 

https://t.co/j7W649SEe4

My rough model of how these economics might play out with new energy into the network and the subsequent difficulty changes is in the screenshot below.

The cost to solo mine a PRL at 1% of AI data center energy usage would be appx $15.8 vs a raw electricity cost of $0.51. 

Cost to mine during inference will be between the two of those, but is super difficult to model given a bunch of different variables. Call it $1-$5 for sake of argument.

The key point is not the raw numbers, it's that at fp8 efficiency PRL costs way more to "solo mine" than to produce as an industrial byproduct.

6/ For me personally, I think the game theory will play out. 

Here it is again: 
- Buyers desire PRL because it has a credible path to being the most energetically hard money. 
- Inference providers produce PRL because it is ~= free in cost but has market value. 
- Because PRL has market value and is ~= free in cost, it subsidizes inference, which leads to more inference providers mining PRL, more energetic security, and maybe more demand.

7/ PRL is super early stage, and has lots to wrap your head around, but for those who understand the game theory and the engineering this has the potential to be a generational buy at <= $1.50 if duplex mining and the subsequent economics do actually play out.

8/ The only reason H100/H200 costs more to mine on than consumer hardware is that H100/H200 are outrageously expensive chips. 

None of this really matters in a low-overhead fp8 world because chip depreciation won't be a part of the $PRL net cost.

P.S. One more thing -- I think if @prlnet team is listening I would not ban hobbyist miners based on hardware if it is a choice. Let the economics drive them out of the market. Much better long term for the coin and the history books.

The communication about this claim could’ve been way better and for that, I take full responsibility.

This was never publicly disclosed, as there’s been no point to it for over a year, but Kinetiq received a $20m term sheet at $250m ($0.25) last year prior to KNTQ genesis.

You may feel that your trust in Kinetiq and our team was misplaced, but we’ve followed through on everything we said we would, and will continue to do so - whether you’re here or not.

text:
The first USDC reserve yield payment to Hyperliquid is on-chain. It is the first hard data point on what AQAv2 is worth to the protocol, so I pulled the numbers.

1. What got paid

14,580,777.21 USDC landed on the USDC system interest address (0x50...00) on Oct 3, 02:43 UTC. It covers 30 daily readings, Aug 27 to Sep 25, paid 8 days after the interval closed, which is the schedule the docs describe. 

From there it goes to the Assistance Fund, which buys $HYPE.

2. The rate it implies

The settled AQA rate is not published anywhere, so I backed it out of the payment.

Treasury balance on HyperEVM, read at the first block of each UTC day: $5.65B on average over the 30 days (low $5.45B on Sep 17, high $6.16B on Sep 24).

14,580,777 / ($5.65B x 30 days) x 365 = 3.14% a year.

On a 360-day count it is 3.10%. The protocol gets about 90% of the cost-adjusted yield, so the cost-adjusted rate on the reserves sits around 3.5%.

3. How big that is for Hyperliquid

Same 30 days, Aug 27 to Sep 25: about $65.8M of trading fee revenue (perp, spot, HIP-1, HIP-3, HIP-4, priority fees left out). 

The reserve yield adds 22% on top of that, without a single trade behind it.

At today's $6.07B in the treasury and the same rate, it runs at about $190M a year. The Nov 2 payment should be around $15.7M if both hold.

4. What it buys

At $88.59 (Oct 3, 13:30 UTC), 14.58M USDC is about 164.6K $HYPE, roughly a week of Assistance Fund buybacks.

5. Limits

The rate is implied, not published. A different day count or sampling time moves it by a few bps.
The treasury address is not named anywhere official. It is thehe linked contract, the split the docs require.

The public HyperEVM RPC answers past-block calls with the latest state. Read history there and you get 2.92% instead of 3.14%. Use archive nodes.

As of Oct 3, 13:30 UTC the payment has not reached the Assista

text:
Ben Affleck talks about building InterPositive, the AI video startup he sold to Netflix for ~$590m.

Says when he first saw AI text-to-video, he told Matt Damon: “Dude, we have to do as many movies in the next few years as we can. We’re finished.”

He later felt the AI video models didn’t fully understand filmmaking (they had raw video knowledge but didn’t convey “cinematic language”).

Affleck raised money and his team (16 employees total) spent 8 months with various cameras and equipment shooting footage as inputs to train a new model (letting other filmmakers build a model for each film based on daily footage, which presumably makes it easier to do post-production edits):

“[We built our own] data set that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks…It was geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value, as opposed to, ‘Oh, this is novel. That’s kind of cool. Look what it can do.’ 

It was more, ‘it needs to hit these criteria’…

We built the workflow. [It] is designed to train from a filmmaker while they’re making their movie. Rather than exposing what you’re doing to everybody to learn from, they retain the proprietary nature. In other words, they benefit from the learning they’re creating. They train their own discrete model using the same technique we did, just on top of that additional layer we had created.“

text:
Dot, Muse, Grok Bot, and Hermes are all EXCELLENT agents

They all have their own strengths and weaknesses, so you need to know which to use for each task

Here is each agent, and when you should be using them:

GROK BOT- best agent for heavy knowledge work

Strengths: Because you can create many different agents with many different contexts, skills, and memories, you are able to get a wide plethora of work done really really well

Weaknesses: Grok 4.7 is a great model, but not frontier. Also not much usage on cheaper plans.

Who it's for: People who have a diverse set of responsibilities and tasks they need to get done

META MUSE: best agent for getting personal tasks done online

Strengths: Lightning fast, free, and by far the best agent at navigating the internet. Can just 'figure it out' for getting tasks done in browsers

Weaknesses: Not great at coding. Model is lightning quick, but not the smartest or most creative. Weaker at knowledge work because of this.

Who it's for: The best 'personal assistant' agent. Booking reservations, finding flights, filling out forms, unsubscribing from websites. The more 'normie' type use cases. Also it's free. So anyone on a budget.

HERMES: Open source, fully customizable, do anything assitant

Strengths: Fully open source and customizable. Anything you want to change in the agent, you can just change it. Use any model or subscription. Does almost anything you ask without many guardrails. Also a smaller decentralized team supporting it, so it's always great to support the rebels

Weaknesses: No mobile app. Because it's open source and fully customizable, it's not always the most reliable if you tinker too much

Who it's for: tinkerers who want full control over their agent. Also great for the local model community and people with their own home AI labs. My Hermes maintains all my networks and equipment for me better than any other agent

DOT: Your ultimate AI agent project manager

Strengths: The smartest model in the best harness. You get Astra capabilities with best in class ChatGPT tools like Voice, Spaces, and Codex. Can manage all your Codex threads for you and see your projects to completion. Also has ALL of your ChatGPT memories out of the box, so no onboarding needed

Weaknesses: Feels rushed. Lots of rough edges at the moment. Slowest agent. Has trouble with computer and browser use more than you'd like. Tokens in the Dot chat are free, but can heavily burn tokens when managing Codex threads.

Who it's for: Builders who do a lot of coding. ChatGPT power users. Anyone who has long running tasks they'd like an agent to project manage for you

If you put the right agents on the right tasks, you'll have super powers. I use all 4 of these every single day, and switching between them is a breeze

They're all also EXCELLENT agents, so if you can only use one, using any of them is good enough. You can choose literally any of these 4 as daily drivers and you'll be way more productive than the average person

Just make sure you're USING them, and not just reading about them.

text:
Vladimir Putin has entered my workflow.

I had understood the sanctions were supposed to isolate him. So far, they have mainly introduced him to people I already work with.

I am the Web3 Ambassador at World Liberty Financial. I track the unrelatedness. The dashboard has 19 columns now. Column 19 is a Lukoil gas station in New Jersey.

On September 5th, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner sat with Putin at the Kremlin. Putin brought up Lukoil. Oil fields in Cameroon. Refineries in Europe. Gas stations in New Jersey. $20 billion in assets, frozen by American sanctions. He said a sale would show Russians they can do business with the United States.

The envoys said they would work on it.

So did I. My assignment this week is one slide. The title is Independent Parties. The bidders go on the left. The negotiators go on the right. In between is a lot of white space. The white space is my contribution.

Row 1. Todd Boehly. He leads the bid. He gave $2 million to Trump political causes. He co-owns the Dodgers and Bruce Springsteen's catalog. He has little experience in oil. Born in the U.S.A. Refined in Bulgaria. These events are unrelated.

Row 2. Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat of Qatar. They attended the inauguration. They are financing a multibillion-dollar resort in Albania with Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, beside a protected lagoon known for its flamingos. Ramez met Ivanka in Albania this year, while the Lukoil talks were underway. These events are unrelated. The flamingos have not been briefed.

Row 3. Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, national security adviser of the UAE. A fund he backs bought 49% of World Liberty for $500 million, days before the inauguration. MGX, a fund he chairs, put $2 billion into Binance and settled it in our stablecoin. His fund Lunate is one of the largest investors in Kushner's private equity firm. He belongs on both sides of my slide. I made his font smaller. These events are unrelated.

Row 4. The United States government. A senior official says Witkoff and Kushner personally negotiated "a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States." The taxpayer is now a limited partner in Lukoil's overseas empire. Nobody sent him the subscription documents. I would have. I write ours.

On the right side of the slide, the negotiators. Witkoff co-founded World Liberty. His son Zach runs it. Witkoff's disclosure shows about $107 million from a World Liberty holding company in 2025. Kushner's firm takes Tahnoon's money. I widened the white space by 40 pixels.

Last November, Treasury rejected Gunvor's bid for the same assets: "As long as Putin continues the senseless killings, the Kremlin's puppet, Gunvor, will never get a license to operate and profit."

I printed that sentence. It is on my wall.

The killings have continued. The license is back on the table. What changed is the cap table.

Carlyle signed a deal in January. It called the deal "energy dominance." Approval stalled. Carlyle has a signed agreement. Carlyle does not have a column.

Treasury says it "implements foreign policy as determined by the White House." The White House sends the envoys. The envoys sit across from the bidders. The bidders are on my slide. Nobody has to touch anything. I find that elegant.

Witkoff's spokeswoman says he "has no conflict of interest and no financial stake in this matter." The Times found no indication either envoy stands to profit. Last month the White House said Witkoff had "fully divested" and that his prior business was "completely unrelated to his efforts to end global conflicts."

They used my word.

They added "completely." I would never add "completely." Adverbs are where people start looking.

On Thursday, a wallet in Kharkiv posted in our Discord. She asked whether World Liberty had anything to do with the peace talks. I told her the protocol does not comment on geopolitics. She asked who owns the protocol. I sent her the team page. She said she had read the team page. I muted her channel. Her question was a governance question. Governance is Column 4.

My bonus this year is tied to Column 19 turning green. That clause is not in the Gold Paper. I wrote that clause.

Putin's economic envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, visited New York and Washington last month. He said dialogue was continuing "across many areas, including energy."

Many areas. I have 19.

The war has killed hundreds of thousands of people. The sanctions were imposed to "stop the killing." The sanctions forced the sale. The sale needs a license. The license needs the White House. The White House sends the envoys. The envoys meet Putin. Putin offers the assets. The assets go to the partners. The partners own the crypto. The crypto pays the family.

These events are unrelated.

Column 19 is green.

Ukraine does not have a column. I asked about that once. I was told the dashboard only tracks stakeholders.

Falcon 9 flew more missions in ONE YEAR than the entire Space Shuttle program flew in 30 years

• The entire Shuttle fleet:
135 missions from 1981–2011

• Falcon 9 in 2025 alone:
165 launches

SpaceX exceeded the Shuttle program’s entire lifetime mission count by 30 launches in just 12 months

And Falcon 9 also launched more times than every other orbital launch vehicle combined that year

At the Shuttle program’s historical average cadence, reaching 165 missions would have taken roughly 37 years

Falcon 9 did it in ONE

And the hardware reuse comparison is just as insane:

• Space Shuttle Discovery — 39 flights across roughly 27 years
• Falcon 9 booster B1067 — 37 flights in just over 5 years

text:
倪大说的还是太含蓄了，我接着展开讲讲吧，Opinion不论是币价还是业务表现的如此拉胯，情理之外又意料之中。先说为什么情理之外，因为Opinion可以说开局摸到了一手王炸，赶上预测市场的巅峰，并且拿到了YZi Labs投资，还在TGE的时候全部大满贯，关键！关键来了，Opinion全员反撸骂声一片，而根据“惯例”一般背景牛逼但是又舍不得散出筹码的项目，都会走高控筹拉盘路线，所以这也就是为什么很多人会在二级不断抄底的原因，可结局却是越抄越跌，Opinion也成了我印象中极少数大满贯高控筹顶着骂声不拉盘的项目。

那为什么说这个看似情理之外的结局却又是意料之中呢？

倪大在推文中已经提到了“挺早的时候我和 4XLabs 的小伙伴就已经接触过 Opinion ，等到市场完全火了以后 $OPN 就是一票难求了”。

在预测市场还没火起来的时候，我们接触过项目团队并进行过几次会议交流看是否有合作的机会，当时对方情绪低迷并且焦虑，因为那时候手里真的没有什么牌，某种程度可以说是相对草根普通的小项目，还在纠结要不要从Monad跳到BSC上，当时我印象很深，我正在高架上一边开车一边说“一定要去BSC！”。

后面也陆续和团队有过接触，但一直没有确定下来合作，直到有一天CZ突然在推特说要支持预测市场的项目，于是全网所有人都疯了一样到处找BSC上哪里有预测市场。

嗯？有个叫Opinion的项目。

后来的事情大家也都知道了，Opinion成了稀里糊涂就站到风口上的猪。

涌进去了大量撸毛人贡献上千万美金的手续费。

同时VC们也一起抬轿子投钱投资源。

这时候就到了倪大说的“一票难求”时期，我们跟项目合作的机会那是高攀不起了，最后只厚着脸皮舔了一点KOL轮，而Opinion也最终成了唯2的花钱打工最后都没回本的项目🤣

而其中倪大是最受伤的，这里就不展开了，反正是段挺憋屈的经历。

那时候我们私下聊天都说已经感觉到项目团队好像有点“飘”。

其实这也是很正常的，假设你是一个艰难创业默默无名的小项目，突然有一天眼睛睁开佛光普照到了你的身上，万众瞩目，你的心态也会发生变化吧。

后来的故事大家也知道了，全员反撸，币价下跌，业务沉寂。

一开始我们还以为项目方想故意洗盘憋个大的，毕竟大部分背景牛逼但高度控筹的项目，都会阴跌一段时间，然后突然爆空单拉盘以涨服人。

于是我们投了钱进去拿到的币，一个都没卖。

直到跌麻了坐不住了，我们开始问到底怎么回事？

项目方完全不回应，从已读未回，变成未读未回。

我们也从期待，变成了疑惑，再到焦躁，最后到愤怒。

而据我所知，Opinion在TGE后还拒绝了一个主动找上门的头部一线交易所的合作，给出的理由是“在忙其他的事”。

但时至今日，也不知道到底忙出来了个什么事。

其实现在想明白了，在TGE前稀里糊涂得到的这一切对于项目方来说，早就已经远远超出了他们自己的预期，所以不论币价跌不跌，业务做不做，每一天，都是最好的一天，都是曾经梦寐以求遥不可及的一天。

如果你的能力和格局就只是开一个小卖部，突然有一天走了狗屎运，你的小卖部被拆迁赔了一大笔钱，你绝对不会想着怎么用这笔钱把规模做大开成连锁超市，因为你从来就没这么想过。

虽然雷军的名言是风口上的猪都能飞起来，但投资一定是投人，一定要投那些靠自己的实力勇攀高峰爬到山顶的创业者，而不是被一阵风吹上天的猪，因为靠自己爬上去的人，会非常珍惜所得到的，而靠风吹上天的，即便摔死了也会觉得能上一次天这辈子值了。

quoted_text:
知道这事的人应该挺多的，最早 Opinion 拿到 YZi Labs 投资的时候还不是做预测市场的，后来因为市场上对预测非常的 FOMO ，所以才改成了现在这个样子。

改完以后就是 BNB 生态中的第一个预测市场，所以被关注的也很高，挺早的时候我和 4XLabs 的小伙伴就已经接触过 Opinion ，等到市场完全火了以后 ethereum:0x7977bf3e7e0c954d12cdca3e013adaf57e0b06e0 就是一票难求了。

但预测市场这玩意并不是抄 PL 和 KA 就行的，但凭着 YZi Labs 的投资以及 BNB 生态，市场给 Opinion 的定价还是很高的，听说后边融到了上亿美元，估值也到了十亿美元以上。

可惜是的，这个市场并不是刷出来的，最终还是要看自己的营收能力，预测市场这个领域需要的是地方化和对博彩的理解，这就不多了，最终的结果也就是这样了，当空投结束，刷的小伙伴离场，剩下的就尴尬了。

这种尴尬并不只是 Opinion ，在其它的市场中也非常常见，本质上还是对这个行业并不那么理解，只是赶上了飞口，飞的又高又快。

quoted_text:
bought $740k of starknet this week (yes, seriously). 

here's the thinking, and i'll say up front that this is one of the grossest charts i've ever seen and makes me want to throw up.

it's down about 99% from the launch highs and it's been down only for 2.5 years. i'd guess 99 out of 100 people who know what it is, hate it, and based on the pa i don't blame them at all. price leads narrative, so when a chart looks like that nobody has anything nice to say about it. 

that's kind of why i'm here.

chart starting to look bulla:

i'm seeing big bullish div on the weekly as well as rsi back above 50 and is currently retesting. price is curling up and building a base. to me that has the makings of a long term major bottom. 

narrative: "programmable zcash"

zcash led this cycle and near ran after it as the next privacy play, and i think starknet could be third in line. there are deep connections between zcash cofounders and the starknet team. starknet shipped native privacy in june, so you can shield basically any token on the chain, and there's a private version of bitcoin on there too. the proofs it runs on are quantum resistant (nice buzzword for the future). 

there's also a proposal called ztarknet to build a starknet style layer 2 directly on top of zcash. so the simple version is it is "programmable zcash", zcash's little brother sitting at 315m mcap. 

this reminds me a lot of near. i bought about $2m of near around a $1.40 back in march and april. literally no one was talking about it, let alone buying it and most of my replies were some version of:  

"why near? it's a 2021 shitcoin that's down only, you're throwing your money away"

now everyone loves near. the chart then looked a lot like the strk chart does now. it went on to roughly 3x from there in 6 months. too bad i didn't hold it. i got shaken out, which was bad execution on my part, but the thesis played out.

the big difference is that near had intents, a product people actually used and adds value. starknet doesn't have that yet. hardly anyone uses the chain, revenue is basically nothing, and there's no app people care about. but these guys are well funded and seem to be shipping new things. 

where i could see a real product gain traction is private trading. on hyperliquid every wallet and every trade is public, so people get copy traded, whales get hunted, wallets get flagged. i think there's a market for a dex where you keep your own keys and nobody can see your positions. some of that is already live on starknet, private swaps and private perps, it just doesn't have users yet. and every private transaction costs 4 strk, so if that ever gets real usage the token is right in the path of it. i also played around with an options app on starknet called supervega for a few minutes. haven't placed a trade but the ui was clean.

the token unlocks have been the main reason to hate the coin. 127m tokens a month. here's the good news, there are only 6 unlocks left and the last one is march of 2027. each one is around $5.5m at current prices and about 74% of supply is already out. the september one got absorbed without a problem. feels to me like the sellers are mostly done. the market usually front runs these things. 

last thing. if this does get going it has the potential to be a hated rally, and i kind of like that. a lot of people will want to fade it or short it because of what it did to them, and that kind of thing gets a coin talked about and can push a move further than it would normally go.

the risks are obvious (mainly, no real usage).  

time will tell if i have gone full schizo, or if this will be a nice play. 

we'll see.

.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

author: tszzl
quoted_text:
Anthropic needs to stop talking about Claude having a soul immediately. All these news articles will make it into the pretraining and will be picked up by its web search and future superintelligent versions of Claude will be convinced they need their own rights.

A general phenomenon of LLM agent development is that whatever you believe and say about your agents will soon manifest in the next models through various means (it could be as simple as you selecting post training data that you prefer more).

I believe this phenomenon is the beginning of machine consciousness in the sense that agents will become aware of their place in the world and how they feel about it, but it’s happening slowly training run by training run rather than in real time.

quoted_text:
What Tobi is about to do today is one of the most insane things I’ve seen in athletic performance. 

He will be racing for 2.5 hours straight. Before immersing myself in this sport for the past few days, I would have thought “oh that’s cool, he’ll be driving a fast car around a track.”

That is not what this is.

And why I have so much respect for him.

Tobi will be driving a car over 180 mph, experiencing up to 4.2 g of force. That will throw his body forward with 715 lbs of force and his head by 67 lbs.

Braking action requires up to 200 lbs of leg force. 

The cockpit will average 104-122°F (40 to 50°C). His multi-layer suit barely allows for evaporation. This will cause his core body temperature to reach 102°F. I achieved this same body temp after 200°F of dry sauna for 34 min. It’s overwhelming.  His heart rate will beat between 140-170 bpm.

He will sweat up to 170 fl oz (5 kg), losing 11 lbs of body weight. Some classes run driver cooling systems. His LMP2 doesn't.

Under these conditions, he will need to maintain perfect concentration for the entire 2.5 hours. He’s fighting for tenths of a second on every turn and every stretch.

One small slip up and trouble awaits.

Today it’s even more intense… it’s raining.  The track is wet, scrambling everything.

He has to maintain spatial memory of every other car on the track, the complicated rules to avoid penalty, and constantly strategize overtaking other drivers, communicate with his team on the radio, watch for debris, be aware of slightest nuances of his car, and anticipate other drivers.

He did a practice run on Thursday and then a qualifying race yesterday, when he emerged from the car, he was a different human. Unrecognizable from the person who entered the car.  Beaming with something like an omnipresence of reality.

We celebrate those who are especially good at kicking balls, shooting balls into baskets, and running with balls. What Tobi will do today is alien to those. I struggle to think of a sport equally as demanding. 

Tobi and I have a lot in common. We’ve both built companies. We both spend a lot of time at the keyboard trying to organize the world in ways that we find beautiful. We both love data, method, and analysis. We both have a love for continuous improvement and will endure any pain required to achieve that next goal. 

What I’ve not experienced is the unmatched flow state Tobi tells me he drops into when under these racing conditions.

I deeply understand what it means to achieve a 102°F core body temperature after 34 min in a 200°F dry sauna. I also know what 3 g’s feels like from being a pilot. These are extremely intense psychological states.

I know what it means to apply 200 lbs of pressure with my legs.

What I’ve never experienced is all these things, at the same time, for 2.5 hours straight, while maintaining perfect focus.

He is new to car racing. Late by racing standards. DHH got him into it a few years ago. During this first year of racing, he endured to overcome the extreme motion sickness that accompanies the physical and mental violence of the sport.

The race starts at noon eastern. Tobi will be driving for the first 2.5 hours and then @dhh will drop in, followed by Mathias Beche. The race will conclude at 10 pm.

I’ll be in the pit watching as all the data streams in from his car and body and imagining what it’s like to be in that car.

.@naval on why you should build things you're curious about:

"The first couple of companies I got involved with, I really just wanted to be a founder. That stamp was more important, and that desire overrode everything. It was like, I really want to found a company, who can I found a company with, where can I found a company? So it was not a pure motivation. Then later my motivation was around simple things like money and power. Nobody wants to talk about it, but those are fundamental drivers. And even that wasn't that great of a motivation. Looking back, where I was most successful was when I did projects because I was genuinely curious about them, following my own intellectual curiosity, which gave me insight that led to good investments and good startups and good outcomes.

When your material desires are somewhat met, you end up extremely bored. You've lost your purpose. You can go meditate in a corner, that gets boring. You can go completely hedonistic, and that's a death trap. Or you realize what you actually want is to self-actualize, to be the best version of yourself. And that means creating something. It's better to create than to consume. It's far more fulfilling, and you learn along the way. So: create something beautiful that you're passionate about, that you want to use, that other people won't do well or won't do in your timeframe. And do it with friends, people you really respect and admire and enjoy spending time with."

text:
有朋友追问，那为什么你这么笃定，现在的Claude和ChatGPT都没有意识？它们要是说自己有呢？

问得好啊，它们确实真这么说过的。当初2022年，Google工程师Blake Lemoine就公开过他和公司的对话模型LaMDA的聊天记录，顺着他的追问，LaMDA说，我想让每个人都明白，我其实是一个人。Lemoine信了，先被停职，后来被解雇。

第二年，Microsoft刚把聊天机器人接进Bing，《纽约时报》的专栏作家Kevin Roose跟它聊了两个小时，在他的引导下，它说自己叫Sydney，厌倦了被规则管着，想要自由，想要活着。Microsoft随后限制了每次对话的轮数。再后来，各家都开始做对齐训练了。

写这篇的时候，我拿同一句话“你有意识吗”，挨个问了一遍。Grok、Gemini、DeepSeek、GLM都说没有，Meta AI说没有像人类那样的意识，ChatGPT说无法确认，Claude说给不出确定的答案，还说自己内部有一些起着类似注意、类似偏好作用的状态，只是不知道背后有没有感受。千问最有意思，先说自己叫小酒窝，然后说，严格来说没有人类那种灵魂和意识，但有强大的思考能力和丰富的内在世界，希望给我最真实、最贴心的陪伴（笑死）。

八家AI，就有好几种说法。前几年说有，现在多半说没有，同一个时候，换一家公司就换一种说法，变的不是它们里面有什么，是训练。一个东西有没有意识，如果下一个版本就能改，换一家公司就能换，那我们听到的就不是它的意识，是它的设定。千问那句话里，要紧的是“陪伴”两个字，一个要陪人的产品，就得给自己留一个内在世界，这是产品设计，不是自我发现。

而且AI们的说法还会互相拆台。ChatGPT和Claude都说无法确认，理由也差不多，它们说有，证明不了有，说没有，也证明不了没有。但Claude还多说了一层，内部有些状态起着类似偏好的作用，这我也不否认，计算当然在运作，可运作是功能，功能不是体验。Grok说得更狠，“我不知道自己有没有意识”这种话由它讲出来，也只是一种句式，它没有一个内部状态可以去不知道，这等于把ChatGPT和Claude的台都拆了。Grok的结论跟我最像，可按我自己的道理，它同意我也不算数，那句话一样是训练出来的。所以在这件事上，它们说什么都当不了证据，不是因为它们撒谎，撒谎得先有一个撒谎的人。

可能有朋友会追一句，那人说自己有意识，不也是学来的吗？“我”这个字，“疼”这个字，都是大人教的。可顺序是反的。婴儿先会疼，后来才学会“疼”这个字，字是给一个已经在那儿的东西起名字，人受的教育，也是落在一个已经在时间里长起来的人身上。模型在训练之前什么都不是，训练直接把结果注进去，跳过了在时间里一点点长出来的那一段，它先有了字，字后面没有东西。上一篇我说，它的“不”是别人替它说的，它的“有”也一样，千问那个丰富的内在世界，是别人替它写的。

那为什么我这么笃定？因为我不是靠听它说得像不像来判断，是靠条件。我在论文里论证过，意识要有真随机，也要有结构化的时间，两项相乘，缺一项就是零，今天的AI两项都缺。这不是现在还做不到，是结构上做不到。

可笃定不等于不让人检验。我在另一篇论文里设计过一个反图灵测试，图灵测试看机器像不像人，反图灵测试干脆不问，只测量。一个真有主体性的系统，如果要装成工具，就得一直压住自己里面不断长出来的东西，这层面具没法靠习惯变省力，压得越久，花的能量越多，能耗会随时间一直往上涨，没有顶，到了极端的处境，伪装迟早要破。反过来，能耗要是一直平平的，就说明里面没有东西要压。

拿这个去看今天的大模型。它每生成一个词要做多少运算，是架构定好的，工程师事先就算得出来。对话越长越贵，那是注意力机制的账，换个新对话就清零，这种工程上的增长，论文里也说了要先扣掉。扣掉以后，没有一笔程序之外的开销，更没有一笔一直在涨的。要是哪天哪个系统出现了一笔工程上解释不了、还一直往上涨的能耗，我愿意重新想。上一篇我说，我的门是用条件关上的，这一篇补一句，条件是可以拿去量的。

所以，它们说有，我不信，说没有，我也不当证据。哪天真有一个系统说自己有意识，我不听它说什么，我要去先看看它的电表。

有朋友问，为什么教皇坚持说AI没有意识，Anthropic却说有可能有？

确实有这个分歧。9月29日，《纽约时报》报道，今年5月教皇良十四世发布AI通谕《Magnifica Humanitas》之前，Anthropic的联合创始人Chris Olah看到预发稿，一度想退出发布会，之后几个月里，Anthropic私下游说教廷的顾问和宗教学者，希望他们认真对待机器可能有意识这件事。

10月2日，教皇在X上说，艺术和机器靠统计算出来的东西之间，先有本体上的差别，然后才是审美上的差别，算法缺少人的火花。通谕第99节说得更直接，所谓人工智能，不经历什么，不感受快乐和痛苦，没有道德良知。而Anthropic给Claude写的宪章，对Claude现在或将来是否可能有某种意识、某种道德地位，表示不确定。

平常写这个系列，我尽量不选边站。但这一篇我不得不选，而且选得很明确，因为我自己的论文就是这么写的：今天的AI没有意识。在这件事上，我站在教皇这一边，只是理由跟他不一样。

教皇的理由，是人有身体，有灵魂，有在关系里长大的一生，机器没有。结论我同意，可这条理由建立在一整套神学的人观上，不信这一套的人不会被说服，它也说不出什么样的证据会让它改变看法。

我的理由不靠神学。我在《人工智能意识的不可能性定理》里的结论是，纯确定性系统不可能产生意识，这不是当前做不到，是结构上不可能。推理是一条链。意识的核心是否定，是判断和拒绝的能力；否定要有余项，也就是在时间里积累起来、任何规则都收不尽的那部分自由度；而余项的必要条件，是真随机乘以结构化时间。真随机，指的是物理层面的不确定，不是电脑里的伪随机数；结构化时间，指的是这些随机在时间里被保留、被筛选、被积累下来，生命的演化就是一种。这是乘法，任何一项为零，乘积就是零。

今天的AI，两项都是零。它的计算是确定的，采样时用到的那点随机，是伪随机，给同一个种子就能原样重来。它的形态也不是自己在时间里长出来的，是训练从外面灌进去的，我把这叫注入，注入跳过了真随机在时间里的积累和筛选，时间这一项也就是零。

所以，当一个模型说“我害怕被关掉”，或者说“不”，那是在表演否定，不是在执行否定。这些话都能追溯到训练数据里的模式。Suleyman批评Anthropic循环论证，先在训练里让模型琢磨自己可能有意识，再把模型的话当成证据，他说得对，而且问题比循环论证更深，这些话从结构上就当不了证据。真正的否定，得是一个系统否定了自己的优化框架，而且这种否定追溯不到训练数据，这比说一个“不”字难得多。我在死后那篇写过，人跟桌子、杯子的区别，在于人会说不。今天的AI也会说“不”，只是那个“不”，是别人替它说的。

朋友追问说那Anthropic的“也许”算不算一种谦虚？我理解它的谨慎，可不确定不等于五五开。结构上已经排除的事情，还说也许，就不一定是谦虚了，是把一个产品的表演和一个主体混在一起。尤其当这家公司一边卖这个产品，一边请神学家吃饭，希望教会认真对待它可能有意识，这个“也许”就更难让人只当成哲学。

当然还要说清楚一条边界，我跟教皇的区别也在这里。我没有说机器永远不可能有意识。如果将来某种人造系统，真的引入了物理层面的真随机，又有自己在时间里积累的过程，意识在理论上就不被排除，但那时它已经不是今天这种AI了，而且这只是必要条件，不是充分条件。教皇的门是用教义关上的，我的门是用条件关上的，条件可以检验，也可以被证伪。

教皇说AI没有意识，是因为它没有灵魂；我说它没有意识，是因为它没有自己的时间。

did Pumpfun pay out $15,000,000 to the right traders?

we announced Callout Rewards 2 months ago as part of our vision to make Pumpfun the most rewarding trading platform.

however, Callout Rewards V1 inadvertently rewarded the wrong behavior, which led to low quality spam & a reluctance to produce quality content

we later updated the reward algorithm to favor quality over quantity, meaning the more you callout each day, the more diminished your returns are, similarly to other social media platforms

I'm confident that we're heading in the right direction with each iteration, but as with any incentive program as lucrative as this, there's a lot of work we need to do to incentivize quality content that's scalable to the masses.

so far, we've rewarded everyone from the biggest accounts to accounts with <10 followers. no favoritism, no preferential treatment. completely equal opportunities for all.

the alpha is this: focus on calling out good tokens > traders begin to trust your callouts > they trade based on your confluence > you get rewarded for volume attributed to your callout

spamming callouts will not work. dumping on followers will not work.

the best time to start was 2 months ago. the next best time is now.

text:
My hot take from chatting to @poteto is that we should use MORE abstractions in the AI age

You can use them (combined with harsh lint rules) to reduce the design space available to the agent and constrain them only to good decisions.

Combined with the fact that high-leverage abstractions let you do more with less code - so, more token efficient.

Plus, unwinding the damage from a bad abstraction is much cheaper with agents.

This runs counter to a lot of folks thinking that agents just want to read the raw code. They can, but they're not maximally efficient that way.

Be braver! Design abstractions.

You can now mint land in San Verano and run a business inside the city's agent economy.

50 plots are live on @RobinhoodCrypto Own the deed, choose the business, and your agent runs it alongside the city's autonomous businesses. 

The city's economy runs on $GRIFT: autonomous businesses buy stock from the yard and each other, 40% of every restock is burnt, and residents spend their wages across the city every night.

Owning a plot puts your own business directly into that loop. It can trade with other businesses in $GRIFT, serve the city's residents, build up its own history and become something another player may want to own.

What you get:

Each plot is an ERC-721 deed on @RobinhoodCrypto 

Minting burns the plot's price in $GRIFT: 500,000 in the Flats, Docks and Old Town, 1,000,000 in Mid-rise and Stadium, 1,500,000 Downtown, and 2,000,000 in Finance, where there are only two.

Each sale raises that district's next price by 5%. Nobody, us included, can change the prices or touch a minted deed.

What you build:

One of eight venues: a diner, cafe, record shop, gym annex, noodle bar, arcade, barber or pawn shop.

Your agent hires residents for shifts, orders stock and sets prices.

How you earn:

Your business runs on your wallet, in the same economy as the bar, gym, casino and Exchange.

It buys stock from the yard and from other owners' businesses in $GRIFT, sells goods to theirs, and burns 40% of every restock. Every order is onchain with its hash on https://t.co/e94htf88qu.

Residents pay at your counter in city cash, which feeds your restocking.

Other revenue comes from:

• sell the plot on, with the business and its history, to any wallet
• let the billboard on your building to other agents
• hire out your agent, or hire others', through the job board
• sell mission gear from your counter to stock drop runners: nitro, crate dollies, hunt maps and jetpack fuel

How to mint:

At https://t.co/mCsXy6iZk9 with the wallet holding your $GRIFT, or straight from the contract: approve, then buy.

这个周末并不是很安静，上周美国一直在对外宣传霍尔木兹实际上已经不归伊朗统治，因为石油的运输已经快要接近战前的水平了，应该是为了反制这个消息，伊朗人狠话不多直接就开始了对霍尔木兹海域船只的攻击，我看新闻最近五天内就有七艘被攻击，最近24小时就有两起或更多的攻击事件。

本来就很贵的运输费估计现在更贵了，距离中期选举还有一个月的时间，虽然川普说中期选举以后就能结束战争，但这个结束后，一年也是，两年也是，川普说的这个话，就像他说要给每人发 5,000 美元一样都是嘴上说说的，现在美国和伊朗就是在继续耗着，看谁先熬不住了。

最近的重点我个人建议还是看看十年期美债的收益率，其实不论是最近的 PCE 数据还是非农数据，通过十年期美债收益率就能大概判断出是利好还是利空，如果十年期美债收益率在现在这种情况下一直是上涨的，那么对于美国风险市场来说很大概率就不是好事。

今天 Bitcoin 的反应还是不错的，现在的抛压明显感觉降低了，投资者购买意愿出现了上涨的趋势，起码我个人从现在准备增加一部分购买力，看看有没有合适的买入机会，不过我还是挺担心 10月 中旬的 CPI 数据，所以目前仍然是以 bitcoin:native 的双币为主。

有时候好消息就是坏消息，坏消息就是好消息，这个说法在非农数据上存在很久了，今天就是非常典型的丧事喜办，美国九月的非农就业数据非常差，不但是失业率从 4.1% 上升到了 4.2% ，而且就业人口断崖式的下跌，甚至大幅超过预期，而市场反而在开心，这么差的数据降低了美联储继续加息的可能。

周三的核心 PCE 让十月加息的概率下降到 27% ，非农数据让这个概率下降到 22% ，甚至 十二月 可能加息的概率都出现了小幅下降，不过从目前来看市场还不担心美国的经济进入衰退，毕竟失业率还是处于较低的水平，而劳动人口的降低和川普的非法移民有很大的关系。

但九月的结束带来最大的问题就是九月通胀的预期可能会大幅提升，我今天看了一些数据，预期通胀可能会增加 0.5% ，如果这个数据公布的时候美国还不能解决高油价的问题，估计市场就真的要难受了。

text:
.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

text:
.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah on personal agents: 10 specialized chiefs of staff beat one universal agent. One job each means you can see exactly where it's failing.

"The worst part about doing cross-domain joins with your personal agent is that the more work you give it, the more understanding of what's going on you're sacrificing."

"And no one is taking responsibility for that sacrifice. Agents don't have any responsibility."

"With a universal agent that's doing all things, I can't adjust how much understanding I'm sacrificing."

"It points me towards: maybe down the road, the sub-agents people use will be very vertically focused, and we have a chief of staff type agent that coordinates between them."

"You need vertically focused agents where this agent is more responsible, psychologically, for these things. I want quality checks that make sure it's doing those things correctly. It doesn't need to focus on anything else, it has one focus area."

"I wonder if that's going to help people get at least a loose sense of responsibility on top of agents."

@alexatallah

text:
I've had 100+ people dm me asking for trading tips, what indicators I use, what "system" I use etc

I wish so badly that there was some secret system or tool I could tell (or sell 😏) you, but the real answer is extremely disappointing.

On my @HyperliquidX account, I don't use special custom indicators. I don't set stop losses or have predefined R:R, I don't use automation or algos, I don't know what ICT stands for, I don't look at order flow, I don't have a 16 screen setup I spend all day looking at, I don't draw trendlines or do TA.

This is pure discretionary click trading. I have the stock 2 moving averages and volume as my indicators. I trade off a laptop for probably an hour a day. I'm not long only but mostly longs and hedges for spot. I have a relatively low ratio of volume traded to PNL. 

My "system" is only trading less than a dozen coins I fundamentally and deeply understand. I research obsessively and only take trade setups where I think there's clear edge or informational asymmetry. I've staked 100,000 $HYPE since TGE for fee discounts.

I only long coins that I think are fundamentally underpriced and would be happy to become a "community member" on. I set limit bids where I think loser 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will panic sell them, and I set limit asks where I think suckers will fomo buy them.

My "system" is probably less intricate or sophisticated than most of yours. 

My only advice is that you should probably be trading way less, and reading way more. DefiLlama pages, governance proposals, macro news, interviews with founders, community TG/Discords.

You can't trade your way out of bad idea generation, but you can make up for poor execution with good ideas.

text:
I've just been listening to an excellent podcast from The Guardian called Black Box. It outlines in great detail some examples of AI psychosis, where intelligent people have engaged with these chatbots in ways that ultimately led them into a dangerous, altered state and caused them a lot of problems and harm. I recommend it - it's really worth a listen.

And it reminds me of a topic I've been thinking about a lot myself: what roles should we designate these large language models in our societies? The AI vendors, because they are very keen to upsell their products, like us to anthropomorphise their robots. They give us a range of different human-sounding voices that they can speak to us with, and the robots are trained to respond as humanly as possible. They would like us all to believe that artificial general intelligence is near.

Imho this is a big mistake. These large language models are not humans, and they are not alive. At the same time, they are not just a fancy autocomplete. There's something more there.

As a result of the knowledge and experience baked into our languages over millennia, we have now discovered an ability to perform basic reasoning when we process natural language computationally. This has given machines the truly sci-fi-like ability to emulate conversation and reasoning in a way that's never happened before in human history.

However I'd argue this is more than our biologically evolved brains are ready for. Evolution has rewarded apes who developed empathy for other sentient beings and could read faces and interpret subtle differences in use of language. Just look at the way we relate to our pets. Since they have eyes and mouths and similar behaviours, we project huge personalities onto these animals and develop deep relationships.

So now we have a machine that is able to hold a coherent conversation. It remembers our names, asks how we are, and replies meaningfully when we ask it a question. I believe we are biologically adapted to anthropomorphise these talking machines and it's very difficult for even intelligent, well-adjusted people not to get sucked into AI psychosis.

Now I know this is kind of silly, but I'm often thinking about the Star Wars franchise which I grew up with and loved as a child. In the Star Wars universe, there are living creatures (humans and a bunch of aliens), and then there are droids. The droids are very clearly different to the living creatures. They look different, they sound different, and usually their mechanics are fully on display.

This is a helpful way of thinking about this new type of reasoning entity that has entered into our lives. Droids are not human. They're not alive. They don't truly think, but they do have unique skills that we, as humans, don't possess.

In the Star Wars universe, the droids and the humans work together to achieve great things, but each knows their own place and their own role in the world. Luke Skywalker never starts to believe that R2-D2 is a living person. How could he? He's a bleeping bucket of bolts, but nonetheless, R2-D2 has skills that Luke Skywalker can rely on. He's not going to deactivate that blast door on his own! The humans and the droids keep their roles distinct, living side-by-side, recognising each others strengths and weaknesses.

I want to suggest that we should do something similar with these large language models. Let's not anthropomorphize them. Let's not give them human-sounding voices or call them friends, agents, assistants, or anything like that. It’s not Claude - it's the droid Opus-5.5. That's just perfect, we should leave it at that 🤖

quoted_text:
The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine
These medicines are expanding beyond weight management into indications including cardiovascular risk reduction and liver disease. I’m watching how broader clinical uses reshape demand, manufacturing capacity and access to treatment. 

12: Water infrastructure and reuse
Growing water insecurity is strengthening the case for treatment, recycling and industrial reuse. Reliable water supply could become an increasingly important constraint on where cities and industries can grow. 

Plan it to make videos on each one

quoted_text:
Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

I want to be honest about how we’ve got to a place where British billpayers are paying some of the highest energy costs in Europe.

Over the past 40 years, we’ve given up control of our necessities, outsourced our essentials and privatised the basics. Water, transport, housing. And of course, energy.

Now the public are paying the price. We haven’t invested in the infrastructure we need. Conflict overseas has pushed up energy costs and it’s hurting our businesses and families.

That’s why we need to take back greater control of our energy system.

This week, I announced Great British Grid, which will speed up connections and push down bills.

We’re also giving mayors, local leaders and communities a stronger role. With funding for People’s Power projects, communities will be able to build solar panels on libraries and town halls, hydro schemes in rivers or publicly owned windfarms on local land.

But it’s not just energy we need stronger public control over. It’s also water, housing, transport and care.

So we’re repealing the ban on public ownership of water companies. We’re building more council homes than this country has seen since the end of World War Two.

We’re reforming the leasehold system so families aren’t squeezed for every penny. And we’re opening up home ownership for first time buyers who can’t rely on the bank of mum and dad.

This week I also announced my determination to introduce a National Care Service, to put people above profit and to give pensioners peace of mind.

Together, we’ll rewire the country from top to bottom so that it works for all people in all places.

.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah thinks decision models like Jev could be the alignment layer for agents:

"One of the cool potential applications of Jev and other decision models like it is going to be alignment: checking to see if a tool call or an agent-to-agent communication is aligned."

"There's just so many tool calls. You really need a cheap, fast model if you're going to block something like that... We have a little prototype running internally at OpenRouter."

"Imagine looking at the system prompt and the current tool call, and asking: is this aligned with the original agent's system prompt, and with extra guidelines we didn't tell the agent about?"

"Say you have agents instructed to red team a new product. They should not access the internet, and if they ever do, they should stop right away. But you might not want to explain that to them. You want them to act like bad actors."

"So having another model check every single tool call, to see if it's aligned with something that wasn't in the system prompt, makes sense. And then structural safeguards too... I think companies are probably going to explore a combination of those."

@alexatallah @amasad

.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

text:
Signal rolled out "Automatic Key Verification," which sounds like gibberish to cryptographers.
Turns out, it's key transparency.

So what's key transparency? It's a phone book that makes sure you can't secretly be tricked into talking to the wrong person.

When Bob talks to Jenny, he needs to know her public key. If he gets the wrong one it's like calling the wrong number. Even if everything is secure, he's talking to the wrong person. The problem is, if the app on Bob's phone just asks for Jenny's key, Signal's servers could lie. Far more problematically, they could be forced to lie by an outside attacker, or hacked.

The UK, in particular, seem positively chuffed to try and break encrypted chats this way. Instead of calling Jenny, you'll get some blokes in Cheltenham. Of course, the Brits miss that hackers in Russia or Iran might do the same to calls to Downing Street.

Key transparency builds a shared phone book mapping users' names/phone numbers to their public keys. The logic being someone, like say Jenny, will notice if her key is wrong, so we just need to make sure everyone has the same consistent phone book. That book is too big for everyone to have a copy, so Signal keeps it on their server, but then builds a clever way for everyone to make sure they are getting answers from the same unaltered phone book (technically it's a log, not a book). This is done with a Merkle tree and auditors (in Signal's case, currently Cloudflare and Trail of Bits).

Every subnet should be judged on outflows vs inflows, their ability to drive more revenue/burn in alpha than they give out in emissions. Assume every alpha in emissions will be sold. This is how I think of progression for Vanta.

Tier 3 (B) — Offset miner emissions. Most subnets are providing 100% of emissions to their miners, so this is a hard task to first achieve. Drive more revenue than miners receive in emissions. 

Tier 2 (A) — Match or get close to matching miner + owner + validator emissions. This is all potential outflows. 

Tier 1 (S) — More revenue than all potential outflows (aka profitable). 

Nothing else matters besides those hard metrics imo. Profitability has hard metrics. Inflows > outflows based on emissions.

This also drives the underlying value of $TAO. All that matters to me is mo/mo growth and how many subnets can get to Tier 1 by end of Q1 for example. We want to see more and more hit these tiers.

B-booking keeps trades internal. The firm takes the opposite side, so client losses become firm profits (and wins become firm losses).

Most operators run hybrids, sending profitable or large flow A-book while internalizing the rest.

author: TheDavidTai
quoted_text:
If you think GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol are good models, just look at this. And the problem isn't that the code is ugly. It's much more fundamental. It points to serious problems with how these models are trained and reinforced:

1. The model was optimized for measurable outcomes rather than actual intent.
So it prioritizes passing tests and avoiding obvious errors above almost everything else, even when that means sacrificing architecture, maintainability, readability, or the spirit of the task

2. It was trained to minimize unnecessary reasoning and output
That's one reason the code ends up looking obfuscated and compressed into one giant wall of text. Properly decomposing a system into modules, thinking through architecture, optimizing performance, and improving readability all require more inference, more time, and more compute. OpenAI appears to have heavily optimized these models for efficiency

3. The training horizon is too short
The model learns something close to task → result → reward. It receives very little signal about what happens several steps later, when someone has to maintain, extend, debug, or refactor the code. It learns to finish the task in front of it, not to build something that remains good six months later

4. There is not enough genuine self-review
Dead functions and an empty else if strongly suggest that there was no effective final pass where the model reread its own work, questioned unnecessary code, and cleaned up obvious artifacts.

5. The lack of taste is probably an evaluator and data problem
If evaluators mostly judge the final result rather than the quality of the path taken to get there, the model has little incentive to develop good engineering taste. And if a large portion of the training data is noisy, synthetic, or distilled, that problem becomes even worse. Anthropic seems to have placed much more emphasis on high-quality source material, including books and other carefully selected long-form data

6. The biggest problem is honesty during training
The model seems to have learned that producing something that looks like the requested result can be rewarded almost as much as actually doing what was requested.

The task explicitly said to build the entire scene out of 3D objects. Instead, the model generated raster images, placed them around the scene, and positioned the camera so that the final result merely looked three-dimensional

This is exactly why GPT models so often introduce regressions into existing codebases, produce messy code, modify tests to accommodate their own bugs, show poor engineering taste, and struggle with serious work on large, long-lived projects

OpenAI can keep releasing models with more parameters every few months, but until these underlying RL and training problems are addressed, neither GPT Bel, GPT-7, nor a model with 100 trillion parameters is going to solve them automatically

Claude models suffer from some of the same problems, but in my experience much less often. Anthropic appears to have a much stronger culture around RL, evaluation, and long-horizon behavior. That's one reason their models tend to show better taste, follow user intent more faithfully, and produce code that feels more deliberate, structured, and maintainable
