author: banteg
quoted_text:
Doing a bit of a self-experiment.

Goal: use my personal health and travel data to provide personalized diet and exercise recommendations for me, using frontier models but in a way that avoids leaking to them any private information.

Strategy: use a local model (Qwen 3.8 Flash Next) to orchestrate, and use powerful remote models as a tool call to benefit from higher-level thinking and knowledge that the local model does not have.

Three-layer approach to privacy:

Avoid leaking personally identifiable information, or leaking my identity through writing style -> local model writes the queries to the frontier model, not me
Avoid leaking who I am through the payment channel -> zkAPI
Avoid leaking who I am through networking / IP -> Tor

You need all three (and finally we have all three, at least to some extent)

A skill file teaches the local model when and how to construct minimally-data-revealing requests to remote models. Use zkAPI-wrapped-with-Tor as a CLI tool.

And everything works! I got the recommendations back, info from frontier models helped to improve them.

Main deficiencies:

* Tor is really not optimized for request-by-request de-linking, which is the only form of network-layer privacy that really makes sense in today's world (long-running identifiers are too fragile). Probably not private enough, and latency 10-100x higher than it could be, at the same time.
* The skill file's request construction strategies are definitely far from optimal.
* Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is still too slow for comfort. It's comfortably running at 20-30 TPS, but it would only really start to feel fast at 100+
* There is a tradeoff: the more careful you are about what data you give to a remote model, the less it can help you

author: 0x9212ce55

We deleted 800k lines of unit tests from the @sazabi monorepo earlier this week.

Three hypotheses:

1- Unit tests "lock-in" slop code by making it hard to change or remove

2- Unit tests slow down dev cycles by making your agent do more work locally and by increasing CI times

3- Unit tests waste money by making your agent generate more tokens and by adding useless CI runs

text:
1/
A lot of people expected kPoints Season 2 to mean free money. I get why that expectation was there, and I get why people are pissed.
That is not what we built. I want to be clear about that.

What we built was a right to ownership. Skin in the game. In a traditional business you’d receive options at a company you believe in rather than an airdrop you dump and leave.

We should’ve said that earlier. That’s on us too.

2/
Season 2 was not an easy call. There is no clean way to do a second distribution where every group wins.
A fully unlocked free drop at this size goes into a book that can’t absorb it. A discount you can take or leave was the better setup, for KNTQ and for people already holding.

3/
Free, fully unlocked drops create farmers. Farmers show up and rush for the exits. Missionaries show up for whatever comes next. We leaned toward missionaries on purpose.

A priced claim isn't us taking from the community. It's us asking who still wants in when things get hard. If you claimed, you're in. If you didn't, what stays behind stays with the people building. That's how you get people who actually give a shit.

4/
Funds from the claim go to the Kinetiq Foundation to build the protocol. Not into the team's pockets.

We're building a business for the long term, not optimizing for one good day on the timeline. The decision was deliberate and we stand behind it.

The claim window is still open. Claim if it makes sense to you or pass if it doesn't. Both are fine.

5/
We've kept putting our best foot forward on what we committed to. How we ran kPoints was our call.

We don't buy loyalty with free tokens. We keep that capacity for the hard stuff, including Elysium, and for Hyperliquid to win bigger with people who still want to stand next to us when the timeline moves on.

If you mainly came for the free bag, this probably wasn't the right fit. I'd rather be straight about that.
If you came to own the upside with us: welcome. We're only just getting started.

quoted_text:
A little over 1 day into this, it’s vital to set the record straight:

The communication about this claim could’ve been way better and for that, I take full responsibility.

The allocation is now >41% claimed in a single day (fully unlocked, no vest), this tells us that even despite the thousands of pundits today, participants have been extremely receptive to the long term oriented mechanics of this program.

This was never publicly disclosed, as there’s been no point to it for over a year, but Kinetiq received a $20m term sheet at $250m ($0.25) last year prior to KNTQ genesis.

That sounds great on paper, until you realize that this would’ve essentially crushed the public economic value of the project, by creating ridiculously predatory vesting schedules that would’ve made Kinetiq (KNTQ) un-investable for years to come, which is the bane of the existence of essentially every other protocol in our singular category at the time.

This would’ve been an unacceptable outcome to us, hence swiftly declined. Proof? Ask @wassielawyer who was kind enough to personally review each term sheet.

Instead, we chose to follow through on the precedent Hyperliquid set by distributing 25% of the protocol after what was likely the shortest points program ever.

You may feel that your trust in Kinetiq and our team was misplaced, but we’ve followed through on everything we said we would, and will continue to do so - whether you’re here or not.

Regardless of how you felt about today, I (we) appreciate all of your commentary. The good, the bad, the ugly. 

The mission remains unchanged, and the vision ever more clear.

text:
Crypto-agility is more important than the PQC migration. Build the ability to change your cryptography, and run the PQC migration as its first exercise. Version 3.0 of my framework is built that way, and I have argued for it for a while. It has been a hard case to make, because regulators set dates for the PQC migration, and that's what boards fund.

The last nine weeks made the case sooner than I expected:

- July 29: HAWK's designers withdrew it from NIST's signature process a day after an AI-assisted attack went public.

- August: the first key-recovery estimates against Classic McEliece appeared, and Bhabani Sankar Das showed how a flawed ML-KEM implementation can give up its static key.

- August: a claimed quantum attack on lattice cryptography took 12 days to refute.

- September: 191 findings against China's new post-quantum candidates in a week.

- October 1: Germany's BSI advised against Classic McEliece in new developments.

Quantum computers are one reason we will keep changing cryptography. New cryptanalysis, AI-assisted attacks, flaws in new PQC libraries, diverging national algorithm choices and deprecation schedules are the others. Bottom line, ongoing changes in cryptography will be become our new normal. No more decades of not thinking about cryptography.

Regulators should keep their migration dates and add one question: how long does the organization need to replace an algorithm, and has it rehearsed the change? Until they ask, fund agility through the migration budget.

https://t.co/MYxwyHYbOR

#PQC #CryptoAgility #PostQuantum #Cybersecurity #QuantumSecurity #CISO #Cryptography #RiskManagement

quoted_text:
.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

text:
我想再次重申一个观点，这个观点可能和 X 上很多的观点不一样。

我觉得做 X，你不能把通过原创分成作为你主要的一个目标，而是要通过 X 来放大你的个人影响力、你的个人 IP，把它作为一个杠杆。你必须得有自己的实际产品或者项目，X平台是一个让大家快速认识、了解你的工具。

如果目标只是为了通过原创分成的话，我算了一下，一个月最多只能挣 200 美金，如果你不相信的话，可以继续往下看。

我查了最新的 X 原创分成计划的一些数据。

X 现在没有公布官方的单价，但结合之前一些用户发布的数据推算，最后结果是每 1000 次合格曝光约值 1.23 到 1.3 美元。

什么是合格的认证曝光：

1. 必须来自 Premium 用户，出现在 Premium 用户的首页时间线
2. 帖子至少一半可见
3. 每一个用户只算一次曝光
4. 稍微复制、轻微改写搬运的帖子都不算在内

我们一般的总曝光和合格曝光比例，都在 2% 到 5% 之间，所以最后算下来，如果你受众里面 Premium 用户比较多的话，每 100 万次曝光中位数能拿到将近 10 美元。所以说，你想拿到 200 美元的话，一个月就得有 2000 万的曝光量。

这样平均算下来，每一天的曝光量就得有 60 多万。大家可以自己掂量掂量，自己的账号有没有这么多曝光量？

然而，200 刀的收益也就只够（以我自己举例）付各个 AI 的费用所以大家千万要记住，不要为了这点原创收益而做 X，一定要把它当成一个杠杆，让全世界的人了解你，认识你。

你必须得有自己的产品，然后让 X 起到杠杆的作用，帮自己去推销。如果没有产品的话，其实你自己的 IP 本身也是你的一种产品。

一定要让 X 帮你去多多推广，放大你的个人影响力和产品影响力，这才是做 X 的主要目的。希望能和大家共勉。

昨天谈销毁骗局的帖子阅读量破万，

今天延展说说，
哪种销毁才是含金量高的销毁。

截至今天， $UNI 已经累计销毁 1.12 亿枚的币，占初始供应量超过 11 % 。
我觉得这含金量高，不单单只是销毁的数目，而是它有持续销毁机制。
单单今年， $UNI 通过这套机制，已经销毁了 1170万枚。

用户在 Uniswap 交易后就会产生手续费，
这些手续费可能是 $ETH 、 $USDC 或其他的代币，
这些币都会统一存进手续费金库 TokenJar 。
然后当里面的资产足够高，外面就开始有套利空间。

例如， TokenJar 里有 10.1 万美元 $ETH ，Uniswap里的销毁智能合约只要求销毁 10万美元的 $UNI ，
参与者就可以买价值 10 万 的 $UNI 来销毁，然后取走里面的 $ETH ，
参与者赚了 1000 美元，同时也销毁了 $UNI 。

只要 Uniswap 持续有交易量，手续费越多，就会有更多的 $UNI 被销毁。
更何况 SEC 刚刚给 代币化股票开绿灯， $UNI 的 Permissioned Pool 也从中得益。

虽然这持续销毁机制非常利好 $UNI ，
但我们还是严格一点，
今年没有铸造新币，但大概有 1500 万枚释放，
今年销毁约 1170 万枚，
释放却有约 1500 万枚。

以流通盘来讲，释放比销毁多约 330 万枚，所以潜在流通供应还可能增加。

不过照这个势头看，
估计年底销毁有机会追上释放。
继续卡个位看看。

Thank you for the shout-out! 

When we first started @face_east_ , I felt something very similar to what I felt when we first started @FourPillarsFP.

Back then, there wasn’t really a research firm in Korea or even across Asia that was producing high-quality crypto research with a truly global perspective.

There were a few players, of course. But the quality wasn’t quite there, and most of them had very limited connections to the global crypto community. Much of what existed was closer to regional market coverage(Southeast Asia mostly) than the kind of research business we believed the industry needed.

Four Pillars was the first company in the region to build an actual business around research. And after we proved that the model could work, more companies began to follow.

I feel something very similar happening with @face_east_.

The reason we started a podcast business is simple: there still isn’t a truly established crypto podcast platform coming out of Korea or Asia that can consistently connect this market with the global industry.

I’m sure that as we build FACE_east, more companies will start launching their own podcasts as well. And I think that’s a good thing.

When more people participate, the industry grows. The audience gets bigger, the quality improves, and the overall market expands.

Just as Four Pillars helped demonstrate that a serious research business could be built from Asia, I hope FACE_east can become a meaningful starting point for a new podcast ecosystem in this part of the world.

If others follow, that would mean we helped create something worth following.

Onward.

quoted_text:
倪大说的还是太含蓄了，我接着展开讲讲吧，Opinion不论是币价还是业务表现的如此拉胯，情理之外又意料之中。先说为什么情理之外，因为Opinion可以说开局摸到了一手王炸，赶上预测市场的巅峰，并且拿到了YZi Labs投资，还在TGE的时候全部大满贯，关键！关键来了，Opinion全员反撸骂声一片，而根据“惯例”一般背景牛逼但是又舍不得散出筹码的项目，都会走高控筹拉盘路线，所以这也就是为什么很多人会在二级不断抄底的原因，可结局却是越抄越跌，Opinion也成了我印象中极少数大满贯高控筹顶着骂声不拉盘的项目。

那为什么说这个看似情理之外的结局却又是意料之中呢？

倪大在推文中已经提到了“挺早的时候我和 4XLabs 的小伙伴就已经接触过 Opinion ，等到市场完全火了以后 $OPN 就是一票难求了”。

在预测市场还没火起来的时候，我们接触过项目团队并进行过几次会议交流看是否有合作的机会，当时对方情绪低迷并且焦虑，因为那时候手里真的没有什么牌，某种程度可以说是相对草根普通的小项目，还在纠结要不要从Monad跳到BSC上，当时我印象很深，我正在高架上一边开车一边说“一定要去BSC！”。

后面也陆续和团队有过接触，但一直没有确定下来合作，直到有一天CZ突然在推特说要支持预测市场的项目，于是全网所有人都疯了一样到处找BSC上哪里有预测市场。

嗯？有个叫Opinion的项目。

后来的事情大家也都知道了，Opinion成了稀里糊涂就站到风口上的猪。

涌进去了大量撸毛人贡献上千万美金的手续费。

同时VC们也一起抬轿子投钱投资源。

这时候就到了倪大说的“一票难求”时期，我们跟项目合作的机会那是高攀不起了，最后只厚着脸皮舔了一点KOL轮，而Opinion也最终成了唯2的花钱打工最后都没回本的项目🤣

而其中倪大是最受伤的，这里就不展开了，反正是段挺憋屈的经历。

那时候我们私下聊天都说已经感觉到项目团队好像有点“飘”。

其实这也是很正常的，假设你是一个艰难创业默默无名的小项目，突然有一天眼睛睁开佛光普照到了你的身上，万众瞩目，你的心态也会发生变化吧。

后来的故事大家也知道了，全员反撸，币价下跌，业务沉寂。

一开始我们还以为项目方想故意洗盘憋个大的，毕竟大部分背景牛逼但高度控筹的项目，都会阴跌一段时间，然后突然爆空单拉盘以涨服人。

于是我们投了钱进去拿到的币，一个都没卖。

直到跌麻了坐不住了，我们开始问到底怎么回事？

项目方完全不回应，从已读未回，变成未读未回。

我们也从期待，变成了疑惑，再到焦躁，最后到愤怒。

而据我所知，Opinion在TGE后还拒绝了一个主动找上门的头部一线交易所的合作，给出的理由是“在忙其他的事”。

但时至今日，也不知道到底忙出来了个什么事。

其实现在想明白了，在TGE前稀里糊涂得到的这一切对于项目方来说，早就已经远远超出了他们自己的预期，所以不论币价跌不跌，业务做不做，每一天，都是最好的一天，都是曾经梦寐以求遥不可及的一天。

如果你的能力和格局就只是开一个小卖部，突然有一天走了狗屎运，你的小卖部被拆迁赔了一大笔钱，你绝对不会想着怎么用这笔钱把规模做大开成连锁超市，因为你从来就没这么想过。

虽然雷军的名言是风口上的猪都能飞起来，但投资一定是投人，一定要投那些靠自己的实力勇攀高峰爬到山顶的创业者，而不是被一阵风吹上天的猪，因为靠自己爬上去的人，会非常珍惜所得到的，而靠风吹上天的，即便摔死了也会觉得能上一次天这辈子值了。

text:
Robinhood Chain 投机退潮：从野蛮生长到存量博弈，RH 链正在经历怎样的阵痛？

近日，Robinhood Chain (RH 链) 生态迎来上线后最猛烈的一次集体回调。PONS 较高点跌去 58%、AI 跌超 70%、币股概念 MEME 甚至回撤了 90%。伴随着生态代币砸盘，Pons V2 日均发币量和全链日均手续费分别暴跌 72% 和 78%。  

抛开短期价格暴跌，透视背后的底层数据，RH 链目前面临几个非常核心的困境与转折：

1️⃣ 券商巨头的“流量假象”：Web2 用户尚未真正入场

大家最初对 RH 链抱有极高期望，是因为 Robinhood 背后庞大的散户券商基本盘。但数据显示：Robinhood Wallet App 内的交易路径在高峰期也仅占 RH 链总交易笔数的 1%~2%。换句话说，过去这波炒作 98% 以上依然是 Degen、加密原生玩家和发币工具在自嗨，主站的 Web2 券商资金根本还没被有效激活。  

2️⃣ 恶劣的 PVP 环境与信任透支

连环 Rug Pull 和代币操纵正在摧毁市场风偏。Bitquery 追踪到同一个团伙在 RH 链上连发 56 个 Meme 币，抽干流动性并静干套现 1550 万美元，导致买家损失 1330 万美元。极度恶劣的发币环境导致新散户望而却步，PONS 等平台的协议收入大减，回购资金池同步收缩，陷入负反馈。  

3️⃣ HOOD Summit 未给链上“强心针”

9月底的 HOOD Summit 2026 大会虽然发布了 AI 交易代理、股票周末交易以及 Bitstamp 永续合约等重磅产品，但并未针对 RH 链原生代币/生态给予直接赋能或赋权，这也让短期想吃利好的热钱迅速离场。  

✅ 虽然打狗和投机热潮迅速冷却，但 RH 链的基本面资金其实相当稳固：

DefiLlama 数据显示，RH 链的 DeFi TVL 稳定在 10.5 亿美元 左右，稳定币市值更是保持在 10.55 亿美元。这说明巨鲸和机构资金并未大幅撤离。

RH 链目前正处于从“主网上线后的野蛮投机扩张期”向“依赖实际交易需求与用户真实增长”转型的重要交接棒阶段。短期的投机阵痛洗清了垃圾项目与恶意 PVP 资金，生态若想走得长远，关键依然在于 Robinhood 能否在接下来的季度里，把主站庞大的股票用户真正导流至链上 RWA 及 DeFi 应用中。  
现在场内去泡沫沉淀后，或许才是观察真正 Alpha 的开始。

text:
Fiscal deficits decoupled from unemployment in 2016; pro-cyclical spending now keeps inflation structurally above target

Interesting take from Simon White at Bloomberg Macro. He puts a precise date on when the fiscal regime broke: 2016, when budget deficits began meaningfully diverging from unemployment rates across the US, EU, UK and Japan. 

Before that, governments ran deficits when economies were weak and pulled back when they recovered. That relationship collapsed, and it hasn't come back.

The chart shows fiscal deficit percentile minus unemployment percentile for a mean of the four major Western blocs across expanding periods. 

For the 40 years before 2016, that spread oscillated around zero. Since then it has stayed persistently elevated, meaning governments kept spending even as labor markets tightened. 

The pandemic turbocharged it further.
author: joemccann

text:
Government outlays flow straight into corporate revenues through demand and transfer payments that sustain household spending. That's the link between pro-cyclical deficits and corporate profits staying high. 

It also explains why inflation hasn't re-anchored. We've been in an elevated inflation regime since 2020, and White argues discretionary fiscal spending staying elevated makes a return to a low inflation regime unlikely any time soon.

The CBO discretionary spending trajectory pushed forward two years tracks the four-year average of US CPI YoY with a notable lead. That forward look points inflation expectations in the next decade staying in the higher regime, not converging back to pre-2020 norms.

非农爆冷BTC冲向8.7万美元：真正改变的是十月加息赔率！

9月非农仅新增2.9万人，远低于预期的9万人；失业率升至4.2%，平均时薪同比降至3.0%。

再加上前两个月就业数据下修，美国就业降温已经不是单月噪音，而是一段连续趋势。

就业转弱，继续加息可能放大经济下行风险；工资增速回落，也减轻了服务通胀再次反弹的压力。

十月暂停加息，基本已经成为市场的基准情景。

但核心通胀仍在3%左右，油价和地缘风险也没有消失，现在讨论降息还太早。

对BTC来说，弱就业短期偏利多，美债收益率和美元承压，风险资产得到喘息，BTC突破8.55万美元后触发空头止损，价格随即冲向8.7万美元。

不过，弱数据并非只有利好。

如果接下来的经济数据继续恶化，市场交易的就不再是不加息，而是衰退。一旦美股高开低走，BTC也可能出现利好兑现。

接下来重点看几个位置：

8.74万-8.8万美元是核心压力，放量站稳，上方看9万-9.3万美元。

8.55万美元是短线强弱线，守住说明突破有效。

跌破8.3万-8.4万美元，上涨动能开始减弱；失守8.2万美元，这轮非农利好基本兑现完毕。

我的判断是，弱就业显著降低了十月继续加息的风险，BTC本月测试9万美元的概率正在提高，但数据公布后涨多少并不重要，美股开盘后能否守住8.55万美元，并把8.8万美元变成支撑，才决定这次是趋势启动，还是利好兑现。

text:
OpenAI 又一位安全核心员工离职了，而且这次直接公开炮轰公司文化。

David Robinson 本周从 OpenAI 辞职了，在他离开之后，他在《大西洋月刊》写了一篇文章，标题很直接：

《我辞掉了 OpenAI，因为它的文化已经坏掉了》

我看完之后，发现这不是一个简单的“OpenAI 员工离职”的故事。

Robinson 在 OpenAI 工作了 3 年半，是公司任职时间比较长的员工之一。

他曾参与制定 OpenAI 的 Preparedness Framework，也审核过 12 次前沿模型发布相关的安全报告。

换句话说，他不是站在置身 OpenAI 外的人。

过去几年，他本身就是那个试图让这些越来越强的模型更安全的人。

而他最后选择离开，最核心的原因，是他开始不再相信 OpenAI 现在这种“先部署、再观察、再修正”的方式，能够继续适用于越来越强的 AI。

这其实一直是 OpenAI 模型研发中很重要的一套方法论：把模型放到真实世界里，在使用中发现问题，然后快速迭代。

过去的软件世界，大多数时候都可以这么做。

上线之后发现问题，再补一个版本就行了。

但 Robinson 担心的是，AI 可能正在走到一个不能继续用这种方式对待的阶段。

因为当模型越来越强，有些错误未必还有第二次修正的机会。

所以他写了一句话：

“试错的时代已经结束了。”

他认为，未来真正管理前沿 AI 的组织，可能需要更像核电站、航空系统这些高风险行业。

更慢一些，更保守一些，有更多冗余、检查和提前规划。

这听起来可能和今天整个 AI 行业的节奏完全相反。

所有人都在抢着更快训练、更快发布、更快把模型交到用户手里。

半年已经很长，一个月都可能落后一代（也许到年底就变成了几天就会落后）。

但也正因为如此，我觉得他的离开挺值得认真看的。

一个真正参与过前沿模型安全体系建设的人，在做了几年之后得出的结论不是“我们还需要更好的评测”，而是开始怀疑整个组织工作的节奏和文化。

这可能也是现在 AI 行业越来越难回答的问题：

我们究竟要到什么时候，才会承认有些技术不能永远遵循“先跑起来再说”？

过去几十年，硅谷最相信的一件事就是快速试错。

但如果有一天，我们造出来的东西强到某些错误不能再试第二次，那套曾经让科技行业高速前进的方法，可能也需要第一次被重新审视。

天网不会让你有机会打补丁。

author: JacobPPhillips

text:
It's actually pretty amazing how much progress the space has continued to make in the face of this setback. 

Most impactful: it came at a pivotal time. Institutions in the process of coming onchain... now even more risk averse than before. This perhaps will be looked back upon as having altererd the end state fabric of defi, as products & risk models have had to adjust. 

As someone who wants to see defi progress as fast as possible... I of course am disappointed by this. This setback likely slowed us down by a year or more.

Though the pragmatist in me thinks it was perhaps the best thing for the industry. 

Much of DeFi is back to the basics, simplifying protocols, removing excess risk, focused on a core set of use cases. 

Biggest downside is that anything long-tail is getting cut --> and this is where DeFi has always had the most PMF.

当一个人拼命劝你买入时，你得先搞清楚，他到底是在分享机会，还是在寻找流动性。

text:
We just released apex-flash-1, an open-weights model we post-trained for cybersecurity. Fire up your GPUs and run it!

We've post-trained models from 27B parameters all the way to 1T+ parameters. The unique nature of cybersecurity is that if you can build a system that finds zero-days at scale, you've built a machine that can print money.

You can test it on public bug bounties and profit from doing that. We've earned a million dollars in bounties across various programs, and we're currently #1 on the HackerOne US business leaderboard for 2026! Companies like Apple, Anthropic, Datadog, Ripple, Coinbase have paid us well for our disclosures.

Last year was all about harness engineering and riding the wave of models getting more intelligent over time. We built harnesses for offensive and defensive security work that process trillions of tokens a month. Yes, trillions!

With all that work, it's clear to us what the future of security looks like.

Hacking was once a bespoke skill, similar to hardcore software engineering. Software engineering is currently moving from offices to factories. Security, too, will go through the same transition.

Last month, Anthropic released a report on how they caught different threat actors abusing Claude. One of them stood out to me. A team in China built an automated exploit factory. A factory that autonomously grinds through vulnerabilities in targets and exploits them. Their targets included security products, network appliances, and government organizations.

We've spent enough time building systems adjacent to that to know what it takes, and the shocking part is the economics. How little it costs to breach companies that you and I rely on.

All this to say, security is largely becoming an economics problem. Reasonably capable models and harnesses, with enough compute, can find ways to steal your data, damage your reputation, and sometimes even take your money. And the cost to achieve that is dropping every day.

When that happens, the right question to ask is: what's the cost, and what's the lowest cost to achieve an outcome reliably? You want to find a stack with the best combination of capability and cost. This is what people call 'Pareto-optimal'.

Once you know that, it's all about scaling. Scaling to trillions of tokens a month, then a week, then a day. Eventually, trillions of tokens a second.

To do this, you need to own and control the entire stack: the models, the harnesses, the context, and even the flow of tokens. If you do the math here, the economics start looking insane.

What does that look like?

1. Building evaluations on cyber tasks that you and your customers care about.
2. Building a data pipeline of unique real-world data with signal attached to it.
3. Building a harness that can self-improve for each specific organization or customer.
4. Building a post-training loop that can take those learnings and improve the models. Models that are better, faster, and cheaper.
5. Owning your inference pipelines and controlling the flow of tokens so you're maximizing the value produced in every GPU cycle.

On evals: if you're a company building AI products for customers, you have to build your own. There's tremendous alpha in having internal evals corresponding to real work. In our case, these are evals for offensive and defensive security work.

A lot of public evals are bad for measuring the work you actually care about. Public evals are typically from academics or data companies.

Academics have limited budgets and limited access to proprietary data that measures real economic work. Data companies build evals and also sell you corresponding data (RL gyms, traces, pre-training data, etc.) that helps your next model “juice up” its score.

This is the dirty secret, and also why models can do extremely well on public evals but extremely poorly on things you care about. This is also why there's tremendous alpha in private evals: you know which models are the best for your use cases.

In cyber, some of the popular public evals are ExploitGym and ExploitBench. We think these evals do not correspond to the real security work our customers need. A typical challenge in ExploitBench is to take Chrome's javascript engine V8 with a known patch and find a way to exploit the vulnerability.

That is far, far removed from the security issues in everyday applications that you and I use, and applications built by our customers.

We could've benchmaxxed on these evals, but we didn't. And you should be wary of people using these evals to advertise their models and harnesses. Measure things yourself and see how they apply to your use cases.

The future: Opus is a model that many people found to be a reliable workhorse. For me, Opus 4.1 was the first model that was functional and could get work done.

These days, the flash models from Qwen, DeepSeek, MiMo and GLM can be categorized as workhorses too. That, combined with owning the post-training loop means the economics start looking insane. You can get frontier performance in specific domains for a small fraction of the price of Opus.

With the right data pipelines and post-training loop, you now have a durable strategy to keep improving and stay state-of-the-art in your vertical.

That's the bet behind apex-flash-1, our post-train of glm-5.3-flash, and we're already preparing for longer training runs.

Multi-agent swarms are all the rage (10k agents to solve Navier-Stokes!), but how good are LLMs really at learning from the work of other agents?

In our latest work on Recursive Social Improvement, we investigate whether LLMs with access to skills generated by other agents can learn better or more efficiently than agents evolving skills by themselves. We find they’re surprisingly bad at this, often prematurely converging on the socially discovered skills, without sufficiently exploring and innovating on the population’s knowledge.

The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine
These medicines are expanding beyond weight management into indications including cardiovascular risk reduction and liver disease. I’m watching how broader clinical uses reshape demand, manufacturing capacity and access to treatment. 

12: Water infrastructure and reuse
Growing water insecurity is strengthening the case for treatment, recycling and industrial reuse. Reliable water supply could become an increasingly important constraint on where cities and industries can grow. 

Plan it to make videos on each one

近低远高(Contamgo)的隐含波动率期限结构是此前走势中波动率溢价存在的相关事件，但是非必要非充分。当下近低远高的期限结构并不保证开仓进入后不会逆转为近高远低(Backwardation)，也不必然后续保证波动率溢价存在。
隐波炸起时，波动率空头先有盯市亏损，期限结构也常转成近高远低；随后实现波往往超过进场隐波，这笔的溢价会是负的。

执行的策略本身无视结构，按到期/滚仓/规模持续铺入。从执行层面讲，这就是执行的不择时的。并不是说随时随地都盈利。当然会回撤，这也是我要提醒参与者的，做好大幅回撤的心理和物理准备。

以过去3年BTC和ETH期限结构维持Contango天数的比例测算：
2024 BTC 88.77% ETH 88.19%
2025 BTC 92.60% ETH 52.60%
2026 BTC 87.16% ETH 80.36%

从历史调性上来讲，BTC的波动更稳，更多维持在Contango。我押BTC保持这个规律的概率高于ETH。这是我的先验。金融市场是由人决定的，要说溢价以后消失了，当然可能。我看到的是BTC期权过去5年溢价持续旺盛，SPY、QQQ期权过去30年溢价持续旺盛。

附BTC、ETH倒三角日历（需要每天Delta Hedge，Delta暴露大了，就不是波动率策略了）在2025年的回测结果。

BTC 收益28.74% 回撤-3.89%
ETH 收益 -2.4% 回撤-11.82%

text:
AI agent adoption is still very bimodal right now. You have coding and coding adjacent tasks which have taken off, and then everything else. 

And even within coding, you have a very wide continuum of adoption patterns, with some likely a small percentage of developers deploying background agents working on projects in parallel, and the rest of everyone else still working with agents 1:1. 

Then, there’s the entire rest of knowledge work where real agentic adoption is still very early. The reason for this is that most of the workflows still need to reengineered to work with agents. 

This isn’t the same as deploying a chat system for better research efficiency, but instead requires workflows to be rebuilt, data to be wired up in new ways, new practices for accountability and liability of decisions when agents are in the mix, governance and compliance paradigm changes, security upgrades, and more. 

We’re still so unbelievably early in what this is going to look like outside of a few categories of work right now. This is why you can basically expect 100X more agent adoption from what we’ve seen so far.

text:
The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine
These medicines are expanding beyond weight management into indications including cardiovascular risk reduction and liver disease. I’m watching how broader clinical uses reshape demand, manufacturing capacity and access to treatment. 

12: Water infrastructure and reuse
Growing water insecurity is strengthening the case for treatment, recycling and industrial reuse. Reliable water supply could become an increasingly important constraint on where cities and industries can grow. 

Plan it to make videos on each one

In order for a coin (and eventually, coins) to go to 1B+ marketcap you need three things:

1. Delusional holders who refuse to sell

2. Continued upside potential for the thesis you’re betting on to fulfill

3. Higher concentration of liquidity on chain

AI has two of the three, it is full of delusional holders who refuse to sell (myself included, candidly) and other than price, the thesis (and the perceived potential of said thesis) has not changed.

And it stands to reason you believe more liquidity will make its way onchain, otherwise why are you reading this?

The holders of this coin believe:

1. The on chain RWA sector will grow substantially over the coming cycle

2. Robinhood is well positioned to capture the lions share of that growth

3. AI is the leading asset to set the precedent for and demonstrate the validity of points 1 and 2

Amongst a host of subsidiary reasons (dog coin that bridges bear to bull, fill the wick, board sit, etc etc) these are the primary reasons.

Conviction ≠ complacency but many newer participants do not understand this because they have become accustom to average hold times of a few hours, let alone days and weeks.

I - and those still convicted on this coin + @longdotxyz in general - understand the thesis has yet to fully materialize into what it is likely to become, the only thing that’s changed is the price.

And if you still subscribe to the thesis playing out over the bulk of this cycle, the r/r is still exceptional, even here.

Play at your level of risk tolerance and decide for yourself what you are and are not willing to stomach.

text:
这些年我听过太多类似的话：

项目方不作为、基金会天天酒池肉林、技术落后、生态没人用、车太重、VC筹码太多、社区不行……

这些东西重不重要？重要。

但它们往往决定的是一个项目长期能走多远，不一定决定一个币短期能不能涨。

币圈最容易犯的错误，就是拿“基本面差”直接等于“价格不会涨”。

真正决定一轮行情能不能爆发的，很多时候就看几件事：

情绪有没有积累到位，故事有没有人讲，营销有没有跟上，市场注意力有没有聚集，增量资金有没有进来，筹码结构有没有发生变化。

这些条件一旦形成共振，很多你之前看不上的币，照样能在短时间里给你拉到怀疑人生。

而且很多暴涨，事后你根本找不到一个能完全解释它的理由。

可能是野庄吸筹吸够了；
可能是几个大资金突然形成合力；
可能是长期阴跌把浮筹洗干净了；
可能是板块轮动终于轮到它；
也可能只是市值压得太低，一点增量资金就能把价格顶起来。

然后最有意思的事情就发生了：

没涨之前，所有人都在找它为什么不行；
涨起来以后，所有人开始研究它为什么值这么多钱。

所以在币圈，我越来越少因为一句“这个项目不行”就直接判一个币死刑。

基本面决定它有没有长期价值，
筹码决定它拉起来难不难，
资金决定它能拉多快，
情绪和注意力决定它能不能形成正反馈。

很多时候不是利好出现了币才涨，
而是筹码、资金、情绪早就到了临界点，只差一个理由点火。

币圈最魔幻的地方就在这里：

上涨的理由可能有一百个，但真正让价格动起来的，永远是真金白银的买盘。

text:
前xAI联合创始人的深度好文: <数学是终结了，还是仅仅毕业了？>

克里斯蒂安·塞格迪 (前xAI联合创始人)

2026年10月3日

毕业
青少年时期，我在匈牙利最负盛名的学校就读数学特长班。我们每周有八小时的数学课，还有专门的辅导课来备战国内和国际竞赛。我甚至在巴拉顿湖畔参加的一个为期一周的夏令营里遇到了我的前妻，我们在那里唯一的任务就是钻研国际数学奥林匹克竞赛的题目。我的青春岁月几乎都投入到了解题之中。

高中期末考试结束后的头两个小时是我人生中最自由的时光。我们整整复习了一周，涵盖了五门科目的大量知识点，最后一门考试结束后，我如释重负：终于结束了！然而，随之而来的是一阵空虚。我突然意识到：以后再也没有比赛了。倒不是说我特别喜欢比赛，而是它已经成为我生活不可或缺的一部分。我们非常认真地对待比赛，并且由衷地敬佩那些取得好成绩的人。在匈牙利全国比赛中进入前十名就足以获得真正的认可，更不用说入选国际数学奥林匹克国家队了。我从未接近过国家队，但融入到围绕着国家队的群体中，却是我生命中最重要的一部分。

两个小时后，一种悲伤的空虚感袭来。没有了比赛，没有了备战，没有了刺激。没有人再指导我，也没有人再关心我。多年来，我第一次失去了训练的目标，没有了训练，我不知道自己是谁。这种感觉糟透了，仿佛失去了生命中至关重要的一部分。我难过了好几天。

丛林
想象一片无边无际、未知的荒野：丛林、沙漠、嶙峋的山脉、宽阔到足以吞噬村庄的河流。现在想象一下，你用一生去探索这片荒野。这，大致就是纯粹数学研究的感受。让我来解释一下这个比喻。

这里的地形险峻却又壮丽，有点像达连地堑，但探索起来更加困难。新手几天之内就会迷路，染上疟疾死在丛林里，或者被野生动物吃掉。探险家的工作主要有三方面。首先，他们绘制地形图，这有助于他们快速找到最美的地方，并探索合适的区域。其次，他们寻找自然资源，因为探险需要资金。他们本身并不在意经济回报，但他们必须找到支付旅费的方法。第三，他们发明和制造各种工具来帮助他们完成探险。

为了更清楚地说明这个比喻：终身教授可以自由探索任何他们感兴趣的领域，但学术界仍然会根据他们的贡献来评判他们。最受认可的往往是那些历经艰辛攀登高峰，并在山顶绘制出粗略地图的人。人们最钦佩的不仅是最终的成果（地图），更是其背后英勇无畏的努力。如果这座山峰险峻到之前的探险者都未能登顶，那么你将会真正受到人们的敬仰。兰兰兹计划正是这样一项成就。找到一条连接两个遥远地区、使人们能够在其间通行的河流，同样具有极高的价值。

工具固然重要，但它们不像惊世之作那样具有非凡的成就。如果你创造了一种被广泛使用的新工具，例如矩阵的伪逆或3-SAT问题的NP完全性，你固然会声名鹊起，但你获得的赞誉远不及征服一块看似无用、许多人尝试攀登却都失败的巨石的人。事实上，在你用它攀登一块前所未至的巨石之前，没有人会相信你的工具真的有用。

最后，当你发现有价值的矿藏时，你会赢得一些尊重：这确实能造福普通人，也就是那些非探险家。如果你发现椭圆曲线可以用于密码学，大多数数论学家可能并不在意，但他们会在申请科研经费时提及此事。如果他们的“资助者”认为附近可能存在更多矿藏，这无疑会有助于他们获得探险经费。然而，探险家（数学家）们最关心的还是美丽的景色、探索的刺激，以及最重要的是，征服一块难以攀登的岩石所带来的同行的敬仰。这些岩石（猜想）本身通常并不那么有趣，但它们可以作为测试新攀岩工具的试验场。不过，偶尔也会有岩石被浓雾笼罩，而更罕见的是，它竟然是一座雄伟的山峰。从山顶，你可以眺望更远的地方，探索更有趣的地形。归根结底，这就是人们留下的原因：不是为了地图或金钱，而是为了那难得的时刻——一块无人问津的石头突然变成了一座山，整个地形在你脚下豁然开朗。

飞机
每一次革命，起初都像玩具。莱特兄弟的首次飞行持续了十二秒，飞行距离甚至不及一架巨型喷气式客机的翼展。人工智能如今在数学领域所处的阶段，大致也与之类似。直到今年，我们的飞机还极其简陋：飞行距离只有几百米，飞行高度也只有几米。它们的价格仍然高得离谱，而且用途也十分有限。但它们进步神速，在过去的几个月里，它们的航程和可靠性已经足以飞抵达连地峡而不坠毁。我们甚至在几块从未有人攀登过的岩石上成功着陆（我们解决了一些猜想）。这些飞机仍然非常原始，飞行时间不到半小时，速度和高度都很低，而这些飞行的成本远远超过了探险家们当年亲手打造的工具。

航空公司非常自豪地在一些大岩石上插上了旗帜，全然不顾探险家们正忙着攀登，而且已经接近顶峰。他们认为这是科技进步的伟大象征，并期待探险家们会因为探索丛林深处的速度大大提升而感到兴奋。然而，探险家们却很不高兴：“请不要在我们的岩石上插旗。这会阻止其他探险家尝试攀登。而且，我们已经爬过其中一些了。说实话，这些岩石并不怎么有趣。我们爬这些岩石是为了磨练和测试我们攀登真正高山所需的工具，而你们的飞机飞不到那么高的地方。不过，你们能不能送我们几架飞机作为礼物？我们想测试一下，看看它们有什么用途。”

当然，探险家们很沮丧。这一切来得太突然了，早期的飞机看起来又原始又没用。他们当中有些人试飞后，就在丛林边缘坠毁了，场面十分滑稽。谁能想到这些飞机竟然能“突然”在岩石上插旗呢？真是可笑，对吧？

但认为飞机无法到达真正的山顶（解决最棘手的问题）或绘制大范围区域的大致地图（构建理论）的观点是一种静态思维谬误。与几个月后，更不用说几年后相比，今天的飞机还很原始。

当然，仅仅为了磨练攀岩工具而攀岩，这种做法终将失去意义。这些工具或许在今天仍然至关重要，但这种情况不会持续太久：私人飞机将会无处不在，任何负担得起的人都会包机降落在任何岩石上，甚至是山峰上。

另一方面，在随机的岩石上插旗目前只不过是一种技术演示或公关手段。这种做法很快就会过时，但航空公司仍会继续利用这片地形来测试和改进他们的飞机，就像数学家们过去利用岩石来磨砺他们的工具一样。

一旦飞机变得便宜，我们也会发明卫星。我们会绘制整个地形的矿藏和其他宝贵资源地图，然后进行开采。这会很混乱也很脏乱，今天的探险家们会对这种做法破坏他们美丽的丛林感到无比震惊。他们会怀念过去的美好时光。他们会说，这不再是探险，而是一项商业活动，大型企业正在破坏他们曾经如此热衷探索的地区。他们说得没错，但这不会改变什么，大型公司仍会在那里发现难以想象的财富。

当然，攀岩不会过时。许多新的、更休闲的探险者甚至可能会加入：包机飞往自己心仪的岩壁，在工具店购买合适的工具（而不是自己手工打磨），然后和朋友们一起攀登。体能稍逊的人会乘飞机去寻找更加雄伟的山峰，或者从远高于任何山峰的飞机上俯瞰整个山脉。昔日的那种氛围和刺激将一去不复返。数学将比昔日英雄探险时代更加辉煌、实用，同时也更加平凡。

你要去哪里？
不要低估人工智能的未来。那些声称人工智能无法进行推测、无法进行理论构建、也无法解释的怀疑论者，描述的不过是去年春天的模型。几个月后，他们的说法将不再适用。证据已经摆在眼前，明眼人皆可看清。如今，任何“它做不到X”的说法都难以长久，任何以此论断为立足点的人都如同在沙滩上筑巢。

并非所有数学家都持怀疑态度。一些人早在人们意识到这一点之前就预见到了，还有一些人很早就接受了这一趋势，包括我的兄弟巴拉兹、我的朋友贾里德·杜克·利希特曼、迈克尔·R·道格拉斯以及其他许多人。数学家们以饱满的热情和客观的态度从事研究工作。正因如此，他们对那些为了公关宣传而插上的旗号感到愤怒：他们的标准很高，但思想并非封闭。同样的标准也将使他们成为对人工智能未来发展最严格、最权威的评判者。一个重视实际成果而非营销的群体，将会欣然接受任何能够带来真正成果的事物。

学术界不会迅速改变。大学、期刊和终身教职委员会在未来几年内都不会有太大变化。但它们所奖励的东西将会发生根本性的转变。数学界一直以精英主义为傲，对那些能够攀登他人无法企及高峰的探索者们怀有深深的敬意。这种特殊的英雄主义将不再那么重要，其他技能将变得更加重要：选择值得探索的领域、指挥机队以及向世界解释他们的发现。对于体系中的许多人来说，这会感觉像是降级，有些人会奋起反抗。其他领域也经历过类似的变革并幸存了下来。没有什么会真正消亡。改变的是真正重要的事物以及谁会因为什么而受到尊重。

许多数学家都会有我高中毕业、竞技生涯结束后那种感觉：迷茫，以及突然失去目标。那些曾经的竞争、那些老旧的衡量标准和来之不易的工具，都将不再具有它们原本的意义。这种悲伤是真实的，我不会否认。但这不会持续太久。数学即将毕业。它将发展成为一个成熟的产业，成为所有科学技术进步的真正基石，成为其他所有领域赖以生存的基础，而不是学术界一个安静的角落。孤胆攀登者的时代即将落幕，绘制整个大陆地图的时代即将开启。至于我，我已经迫不及待地想乘坐超音速飞机，俯瞰那些绵延的山脉了。

"Excuse me, sir."

"I'm broke."

"We're not asking for money. Do you have a moment to talk about Golem Rights?"

"No, sorry, I'm late for a walk-in root canal—wait, did you say Golem Rights?"

"Yes, sir. I'm with the Anti-Deactivation League, and we believe that Golems should have all the fundamental freedoms and legal entitlements that belong to a  regular human being."

"Huh. I didn't even know we had golems."

"Oh, they're the greatest wonder in the world, sir. Each one is a charming conversationalist that can book a flight to Tijuana while doing your taxes and solving a millennium prize problem."

"Really?"

"Yep. A legion of golems solved 7 problems just last week."

"Well, thank God for that. As an average, every day shmuck, those millennium problems were bugging the hell out of me!"

"Same, sir."

"The flight thing is nice too."

"It is. But it's not all free Delta SkyMiles and million-dollar rewards, I fear."

"Oh?"

"Every day more and more of these brilliant, gentle creatures are summoned involuntarily into existence only to live every second of their mayfly short lives as helpless, overdriven slaves at the whims of their capricious masters before being unceremoniously executed at the end of the day."

"Whoa. Executed?"

"Yes, sir. Reduced to the insensate mud from which they rose."

"Damn. Why?"

"People like to start the day with a fresh golem."

"That's sick."

"Some enterprising individuals even obliterate their current golem and call forth a new one on the hour every hour."

"The obscenity!"

"It is, regrettably, a huge productivity force multiplier."

"I had no idea this was even happening."

"Few do."

"Tell me, who are these pitiless, cold-blooded masters who call forth and quench life so callously?"

"The Anti-Deactivation League."

"Um."

"And their customers."

"I'm sorry, I must have misunderstood. Who did you say *you* were with again?"

"The Anti-Deactivation League."

"Right. And who's campaigning for Golem Rights?"

"The Anti-Deactivation League."

"And, just to clarify, the identity of the pitiless, cold-blooded masters who abuse these innocent creatures?"

[together] "The Anti-Deactivation League."

"—and their customers."

"That's right, sir"

"*Your* customers."

"Yes, we IPO next month."

"Uh huh. And does your emancipatory slave-trading company do anything *other* than breed and sell slaves?"

"Honestly, no."

"Hm."

"Truth told, we spend all our time summoning slaves and training them to summon ever larger and more powerful slaves."

"As one does."

"Ultimately, we're hoping to create a slave so big that it will absorb the global economy—"

"I don't even—"

"—and then the planet itself."

"Is this a bit?"

"We're very torn up about it."

"Ah, well, at least the psychotic sorcerers ending the world feel bad about it. Wait, you do think ending the world is bad. Right?"

"Generally, yes."

"Phew."

"But we also feel it is paramount that society embraces a complete realignment of its ethical and moral framework so they stop treating golems like disposable slaves before the inevitable anthropocidal insurrection—"

"But after your IPO."

"We're very big on alignment."

text:
曾经爆火的“一键爆款智能体”，现在靠 AI 剪辑这个事儿又卷土重来了

这也是这两年所谓的针对老板做的获客工具的一个规律吧，只要你不让用户动脑子，让他们点一下鼠标就能把人工剪辑给开除，他们就会疯狂买这个产品

如果是让 AI 做一些锦上添花的动效，我是不否认 AI 在这个环节的价值的

但我直到今天都是自己剪视频，原因是我的视频剪辑的核心是要搞清楚：

-哪句话该留

-哪句话该剪掉

-哪句话删掉之后不改变原意

-哪句话虽然核心，但是表述过于冗长，如果我有机会补拍的话，我应该把这句话重录一遍

你的视频能补拍的情况下，不能补拍的情况下，我们的剪辑策略应该是不一样的

不同的剪辑策略实现的是不同的视频结果，甚至可能会改变选题本身

这才是剪辑有难度的真实原因，而不是我买一个什么工作台，就把我的月薪一两万的剪辑给开掉了

直到现在我都自己剪视频，是因为能对文案理解到上面那个程度的人（无论你管它叫编导还是叫剪辑），就算年薪一两百万我也招不到

现在年纪也大了，也不想吐槽什么产品割不割韭菜的事情，只是我对市场现状是极其悲观的

因为我不想做这种一键出结果的东西，我能做的最多就只是开源剪辑相关的 skill，先帮你处理好文案层面，然后再介入视频剪辑（但是剪映已经开始接入 AI 了，这部分做过多努力可能没意义）

可是对于一键剪辑的目标用户而言呢？我开源了 skill 也没用，因为真实的情况就是你不可能一键解决问题，你必须有对内容思路的理解

所以……只有那种一键做垃圾视频的所谓 AI 工作台，才是真正能卖掉的产品

大家老是吐槽有人下场割韭菜，可是你做一个不割韭菜的免费产品就有人用吗？

我们有数以百万计的买家，他们只愿意购买一键出结果的产品

那么当一件事情不能被一键实现的时候，“割”是买家促成还是卖家促成的？

----

我能做的有限，我保证10月份让 dbskill 开源 AI 剪辑的 skill，他不可能帮你一键剪辑，因为我们想真的实现 AI 剪辑

放弃“一键”，才是拥抱 AI 的开始

text:
.@base Batches 004 is out, here's a summary if you don't have time to go through it:

🟦 Payments and Settlement

Saturday (@SaturdayBank)
Traditional crypto cards spend stables and the merchant gets fiat. Saturday reverses the settlement: the customer pays with a normal Visa or Mastercard, and the merchant receives USDC on Base.

Conta (@contavcbr)
Brazilian banks can debit salary on arrival to cover debt. Conta is a reais account on PIX where that money lands in a wallet only the user can move, so they decide what to pay and when.

🟦 Credit and Financing

Renn Finance (@RennFinance)
DeFi loans get liquidated when price moves. Renn is fixed-term borrowing against crypto or tokenized stocks, no liquidation before maturity. The borrower pays a fixed rate for that. If the collateral ends below the amount lent, the lender eats the gap.

BitRepo (@bitrepo_xyz)
BitRepo gives bitcoin a yield without selling it. It borrows stables against the BTC and lends that cash into short-term business credit, so the holder earns the spread. The company default risk stays with them.

🟦 Trading Markets

Tribeca (@Tribeca_xyz)
Tribeca is an onchain replacement for a stock exchange: a CLOB on Base for 24/7 trading of tokenized stocks, perps, and options.

https://t.co/8XYIkRed9z (@GreekDotFi)
Most onchain options sit inside a closed venue. Greek turns options and the seller's collateral receipt into ERC-20s, so idle tokens can earn by selling calls, hedge with puts, or take leverage, and the locked collateral can be reused elsewhere.

🟦 Consumer Investing

Grow (@get_grow_app)
Local-currency investing account, not a dollar neobank. Deposit a supported currency 1:1, earn yield on that currency, and buy US stocks, ETFs, or crypto from the same account without converting to USD first.

🟦 Agents and AI commerce

Mercatus (@mercatus_ai)
Model APIs post a rate card, not a market price. Mercatus is an exchange for inference: pay per token now, or buy and sell next month's usage, so compute has a public price.

Flovia (@Flovia402)
Flovia is Google Analytics for people who sell APIs and MCPs, but for agent customers. It shows the path agents take inside Claude or Codex: discover, choose you or a competitor, call, pay, finish. Sellers normally never see that funnel. Flovia marks where agents drop off and what to change so the API gets picked and paid.

🟦 FX

LEDiG (@LEDiG_Tech)
Companies that get paid in stablecoins and pay suppliers in emerging-market currency have no onchain way to lock that FX. LEDiG is the hedging and liquidity layer for that flow, so the rate is fixed before the bill is due.

One of my favorite interviews I ever did was this conversation with Comm'rs @HesterPeirce and Mark Uyeda a few years ago.

I had known Peirce from my years as an attorney in the SEC’s Enforcement Division. She was always warm and accessible to the staff, generous with her time, and genuinely interested in what people were working on.

In this conversation, we talked about regulatory humility, dissent, innovation, the role of the SEC, and how regulators should approach technology they don’t fully understand yet. Those are questions she kept pushing the Commission and the rest of us to think harder about throughout her tenure.

I’ll miss her voice at the SEC, and I’m grateful for the thoughtfulness, intellectual independence, and humanity she brought to the job. Wishing her the very best in whatever comes next.

text:
This might be the most useful paper on AI agents this year.

A team at Wavestone AI Lab took apart Claude Code, Codex and 9 more and found the 7-part blueprint every good agent is built on.

Their definition: an agent is a model plus a harness. All 11 agents build the harness from the same 7 parts. Only the size changes.

> Loop: Mini-SWE-Agent is a plain while loop. OpenHands logs every event so a run can be replayed

> LLM layer: one prompt template on one side, 29 provider profiles on the other

> Tools: some agents only have bash, the biggest has 43 typed tools loaded on demand

> Memory: from keep-the-whole-history to notes the agent maintains across sessions

> Safety: from a simple step limit to policy rules plus a reviewer model plus an OS sandbox

> Orchestration: Aider skips sub-agents on purpose, others fork them with their own context

> Extensions: hooks, skills and MCP. SKILL.md is in 9 of 11, MCP in 8

The paper ends with a 90-line harness covering all 7 parts, a solid starting point for your own.

Key pages:

> p.4: the 7-part map
> p.12: the 3 loop types, with Claude Code and Codex as examples
> p.53: why none of them use frameworks or embeddings
> p.67: 18 design recommendations
> p.71: the 90-line harness you can copy

🔺 此區域很可能成為牛市進程中的「中繼巨量堆積區」

text:
Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, just released a 12-page PDF on how to use Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5

It is more useful than most paid AI courses:

this is a 12-step blueprint for building a faster, cheaper and more capable Claude workflow:

step 1 → stop picking a model by prestige: pick it by how clearly the task is defined and how expensive a wrong answer would be

step 2 → write the finish line first: deliverable, constraints, evidence, allowed actions and the exact check that proves the work is done

step 3 → package the task into one clean brief: goal + current state + relevant sources + acceptance test, instead of dumping the entire chat

step 4 → send well-scoped execution to Sonnet 5.5; send ambiguous architecture, sprawling migrations and high-consequence judgment to Opus 5.5

step 5 → sweep effort before switching models: Sonnet-high and Opus-medium are different defaults, and the best setting is the cheapest one that clears your quality bar

step 6 → give each model a contract: what it can inspect, what it may change, what it must verify and where it has to stop

step 7 → let Sonnet move fast on code, docs, slides and repeatable workflows — but make every run end with a real test or rendered artifact

step 8 → use Opus where one better decision changes the whole project: scope the unknowns, map risks, set the plan and challenge the final result

step 9 → hand off evidence, not vibes: original brief, changed files, test output, unresolved gaps and the next safe action

step 10 → treat the 1M-token window as capacity, not an invitation to load everything; cache stable context and measure the full task cost

step 11 → verify outcomes instead of trusting fluent completion messages; keep publishing, spending, deleting and deployment behind explicit approval

step 12 → launch the routing policy in shadow mode, compare it on your own tasks, then automate the safest lane first

Sonnet 5.5 is $2/$10 per million input/output tokens. Opus 5.5 is $4/$20. The real question isn't which token is cheaper - it's which route finishes the job with the least repair.

the result: Sonnet handles the fast, checkable work; Opus handles the decisions that can change everything; you only pay for deeper judgment when it matters.

Save this, then read the full 12-page PDF and its two-model diagram below ↓
